title: A Legacy of Leadership and Hope: The Elaine and Eduardo Saverin Foundation’s generational commitment to patients with metastatic breast cancer
body:
Spring 2026
By Amber Sinicrope
Photography by Bryce Vickmark

The Elaine and Eduardo Saverin Foundation has made an extraordinary $20 million grant to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute to accelerate research and care for people living with stage IV breast cancer. The Foundation’s new grant, combined with the Saverin family’s 2019 commitment establishing the Saverin Fund for Metastatic Breast Cancer Research, constitutes the largest non-federal grant in metastatic breast cancer at Dana-Farber, a critical area where there are not yet cures. The Saverin family’s relationship with Dana-Farber is rooted in a deep commitment to accelerating research in late-stage breast cancer and compassionate, patient-centered care. Their tremendous 2019 gift built a translational and data backbone for metastatic research, expanded biomarker-driven, patient centered studies, and helped grow patient care programs such as EMBRACE (Ending Metastatic Breast Cancer for Everyone). The Elaine and Eduardo Saverin Foundation’s new grant accelerates the promise of precision oncology, so that the right therapies reach patients with advanced disease faster.

Metastatic breast cancer patients are often left on the margins of cancer treatment conversations, yet they live with incredible courage and complexity.

Elaine Saverin, Elaine and Eduardo Saverin Foundation

“Metastatic breast cancer patients are often left on the margins of cancer treatment conversations, yet they live with incredible courage and complexity,” said Elaine Saverin, co-founder of the Foundation. “Our goal is to enable Dana-Farber to continue to make a significant impact on the treatments available to and the long-term outcomes for people living with late-stage breast cancer.”

The new funding will strengthen clinical trials to identify biomarkers of response and resistance in metastatic breast cancer and rapidly translate promising preclinical strategies into patient studies. It will expand infrastructure to integrate and analyze clinical, genomic, and imaging data from more than 20,000 patients and harness AI to predict outcomes, personalize therapies, understand tumor–immune interactions, and identify resistance mechanisms. The grant will also advance the growing field of liquid diagnostics and fuel work in using circulating tumor DNA to catch recurrence earlier and tailor treatment accordingly, while continuing the Saverin Research Awards that empower physician-scientists to pursue bold ideas poised to have an impact on the landscape of metastatic breast cancer research. Leading Dana-Farber’s breast oncology program is Sara Tolaney, MD, MPH, chief of the Division of Breast Oncology and recent recipient of the AACR Outstanding Investigator Award for Breast Cancer Research in recognition of her groundbreaking work personalizing treatment for people with breast cancer.

“With the Foundation’s support, we will endeavor to identify more efficacious therapies to treat stage IV breast cancer and develop innovative technologies to accelerate our progress and improve patient experiences with metastatic disease,” said Tolaney. Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD, president and CEO at Dana-Farber and the Richard and Susan Smith Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, added, “This extraordinary grant will allow Dana-Farber to accelerate our approach to improve the treatment and care of metastatic breast cancer.”

Founded in 2023, the Elaine and Eduardo Saverin Foundation supports education, healthcare, mental health, and wildlife conservation and regenerative futures. This signature contribution reflects their healthcare mission to spark hope and support compassionate care for patients everywhere.

title: Jimmy Fund Walk steps into record-breaking year with over $11.2 million raised
body:
Spring 2026
By Robbie Merritt

On a sunny Sunday in October 2025, the Jimmy Fund Walk presented by Hyundai,  Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s signature fundraising event, crossed more than just the finish line at Boston Common. For the first time in its 37 years of fundraising, the Walk passed the $10 million threshold, raising more than $11.2 million and bringing its lifetime total to over $197 million raised for groundbreaking research and patient care at Dana-Farber.

Apart from the monumental fundraising milestone, the Walk also saw exceptional participation numbers. More than 9,300 walkers and 1,000 volunteers, made up of patients, families, nurses, doctors, and supporters, came together against cancer on the famed Boston Marathon® course, keeping energy high and helping to drive the massive success. Regardless of which distance they chose—5K, 10K, half marathon, or full marathon—participants were greeted by cheer squads lining the streets and motivational messages on every corner, like the Hero posters that feature photographs and inspirational quotes from adult and pediatric patients. Many walkers also joined virtually from their own communities.

All routes concluded at the Jimmy Fund Walk Finish Line powered by Schneider Electric at Boston Common, the nation’s oldest public park, where a lively celebration awaited finishers. There was music, food, and beverages courtesy of generous sponsors, and impactful speeches from Dana-Farber leadership, patients, and presenting sponsor Hyundai, which has supported the Walk since 1998.

Simply said, the money raised offers a chance at life. That’s the real bottom line.

Barbara Gubb

Also celebrating a milestone year was walker Barbara Gubb, who reached $250,000 in cumulative funds raised. Barbara had been volunteering at Dana-Farber for some time before finding out about the Walk, and between seeing firsthand the incredible care patients receive and experiencing personal brushes with cancer, Barbara knew she had to be part of the solution.

“In 2009, my sister, Natalie, was diagnosed with ovarian cancer, and my good friend Janet learned she had breast cancer. Around the same time, I discovered that I shared my late sister’s BRCA gene mutation and immediately turned to Dana-Farber for examination and treatment,” Barbara recalled. “All that motivated me to start walking in the Jimmy Fund Walk, and I haven’t stopped since.” Now, Barbara can’t imagine not walking. “The more I walk, the more important it becomes in my life,” she said. “While it helps fund research and treatment, the truth is that I get as much, if not more, in return. The Walk gives me a purpose unlike most other activities.”

Reflecting on her 17 years as a walker, Barbara celebrates her efforts and acknowledges the impact of supporting cancer care and research. “I’m very proud to have generated $250,000 over the years, but just as much credit goes to my friends and family who have been extremely generous,” she said. “Events like the Jimmy Fund Walk are so important because the funds go directly to critical research and care, creating optimism, hope, and, in many cases, survival for patients and families. Simply said, the money raised offers a chance at life. That’s the real bottom line.”

title: An un-fore-gettable year with Jimmy Fund Golf
photo_credit: Photography by Maura Wayman, Samantha Paige Photography, Bryce Vickmark, Allie Joseph
body:
Spring 2026
By Elyse Pleickhardt
Photography by Maura Wayman, Samantha Paige Photography, Bryce Vickmark, Allie Joseph

For more than 43 years, Jimmy Fund Golf presented by Mohegan Sun has brought together more than 20,000 golfers on fairways across the country to advance Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s lifesaving mission. In 2025, 140 Jimmy Fund Golf events raised more than $6.5 million for cancer care and research—simply by doing what they love. “Jimmy Fund Golf tournament directors and committees work tirelessly within their own communities,” said Caitlin Fink, vice president of the Jimmy Fund. “By rallying friends, family, colleagues, and local businesses, they turn passion into fuel that makes a difference in the lives of so many at Dana-Farber and beyond.” Jimmy Fund Golf is grateful to all its tournament directors, volunteers, and supporters for transforming the game of golf into something communal, powerful, and lifechanging.

Learn more about all 2025 tournaments.

title: Levy gift supports Dana-Farber’s vision for the future of cancer care
body:
Spring 2026
By Caitlin Henault

When Sarah Salter Levy and Steven Levy learned of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s plans to build New England’s first inpatient hospital dedicated to adults with cancer, they wanted to be among the first to step forward with philanthropic support. Scheduled to serve patients in 2031 in Boston’s Longwood Medical Area, Dana-Farber’s planned cancer hospital will encompass 450,000 square feet devoted to patient care, including 300 private inpatient rooms, 30 licensed ICU beds, and a 16-bed observation suite. The hospital will also inaugurate a new clinical partnership between Dana-Farber and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC).

As longtime supporters of BIDMC, the Levys eagerly embraced this visionary partnership to elevate the standard for cancer care in New England. With a $3 million gift to Dana-Farber’s Future of Cancer Care Fund, the Levys have provided Dana-Farber with funds that will accelerate the development of the future of cancer hospital and innovative services that will define the patient experience, bolster our research enterprise, expand access to care, and improve outcomes for patients with cancer.

“Dana-Farber’s future cancer hospital is perhaps the most transformative opportunity in the medical community that I’ve ever seen—not just in Boston, but in the United States,” said Steven. “We couldn’t pass up the chance to support not just a new building, but what it represents: a powerful collaboration between two of Boston’s best institutions to elevate cancer care for generations to come.”

Designed to adapt to rapid advances in oncology and meet the growing increase in cancer diagnoses, Dana-Farber’s state-of-the-art facility will ensure that patients have timely access to innovative clinical trials, world-class clinical care, and breakthrough therapies tailored to their individual needs. With direct pathways to Dana-Farber’s Yawkey Center for Cancer Care and research enterprise, as well as BIDMC’s broad range of surgical and other specialists, the hospital will enhance Dana-Farber’s visionary total patient care model, delivering seamless, comprehensive, specialized care and personalized treatment protocols directly to each patient’s bedside. “We’re firm believers that sharing information between institutions only helps the greater good,” said Sarah. “We’ve been connected to BIDMC for decades, and we knew now was the perfect time to show our support for Dana-Farber and the tremendous work they are doing as well.”

Dana-Farber’s future cancer hospital is perhaps the most transformative opportunity in the medical community that I’ve ever seen—not just in Boston, but in the United States.

Steven Levy

“When we first shared this vision with Sarah and Steven, their enthusiasm was palpable and inspiring,” says Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD, president and CEO of Dana-Farber and the Richard and Susan Smith Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School. “Visionary philanthropy from supporters like the Levys is essential to bringing our innovative care model to life. Together, we will expand what’s possible in cancer care and research—enabling more patients to receive integrated, best-in-class inpatient and outpatient care.”

title: Your generosity on GivingTuesday is fueling the next victory over cancer
body:
Spring 2026
By Stephanie Lowitt

In 2012, GivingTuesday was created with one simple goal: encourage generosity and collective giving. What was once a small experiment in communal impact is now a worldwide movement comprised of donors who support causes close to their hearts.  

Dana-Farber and the Jimmy Fund participated once again in 2025, with over 8,000 supporters across the country donating more than $2.6 million, surpassing the previous record of $2.4 million. This new level of generosity will fuel the next breakthrough research discoveries, lifesaving care, and victories against cancer. Longtime supporter Arbella Insurance Group helped inspire donors by tripling all gifts made, up to $50,000, through midnight on Dec. 2. 

The majority of GivingTuesday gifts provide flexible, unrestricted funding that supports Dana-Farber’s investment in transformational research and the most urgent organizational needs. These contributions allow Dana-Farber to be nimble, take advantage of new opportunities, and provide even more vital support to patients and their families.

On GivingTuesday, the Dana-Farber and Jimmy Fund community heard the story of Capri, one of the many patients who have benefited from donors’ support.

Hearing Capri’s cancer diagnosis was devastating, and living through treatment was heartbreaking at times. But Dana-Farber carried us through our darkest moments. As a family, we learned how strong we really are, and we cherish every smile, laugh, and milestone with Capri even more than before.

La’Shee, mother of pediatric patient Capri

At just seven months old, Capri was diagnosed with stage III rhabdomyosarcoma, a rare type of highly aggressive cancer that begins in soft tissue. When her family came to Dana-Farber for help, we were able to provide them with the latest treatment innovations and compassionate care. After treatment that included tumor removal, reconstructive surgery, radiation, and 30 rounds of chemotherapy, Capri is now cancer-free, and her family could not be more grateful.

“Hearing Capri’s cancer diagnosis was devastating, and living through treatment was heartbreaking at times. But Dana-Farber carried us through our darkest moments. As a family, we learned how strong we really are, and we cherish every smile, laugh, and milestone with Capri even more than before,” says Capri’s mother La’Shee. On behalf of everyone who turns to Dana-Farber for hope and healing, thank you to everyone who has made a gift on GivingTuesday or throughout the year—your ongoing generosity is saving lives.

title: Alex’s Lemonade Stand Foundation continues steadfast support
body:
Spring 2026
By Lisa Gregory

The legacy of a remarkable little girl has guided the mission of Alex’s Lemonade Stand Foundation (ALSF) since it was established in 2005. When Alex Scott was 4 years old, she held lemonade stand fundraisers to help other children like her with cancer. After her passing at the age of 8, Alex’s parents established ALSF in her memory to advance cancer research.

This year, in 2026, we mark the 20th anniversary of when ALSF’s generous support began for Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, totaling more than $22 million. ALSF granted more than $1.8 million in Young Investigator Awards in 2024 and 2025 to five Dana-Farber researchers in pediatric oncology. “Changing the lives of children with cancer is at the heart of our mission,” said Liz Scott, Alex’s mother and the co-executive director of ALSF. “We are excited about the groundbreaking research being done at Dana-Farber and the impact it can have for all kids.”

Daniel Solvie, PhD, received funding to conduct research on neuroblastoma, or cancer of the nerve cells. His focus is to identify a natural mechanism to turn off the MYC gene in cancer cells, an active player in many aggressive cancer subtypes, which may lead to less toxic childhood treatments.

We are excited about the groundbreaking research being done at Dana-Farber and the impact it can have for all kids.

Liz Scott, Alex’s Lemonade Stand Foundation

Shuhei Asada, MD, PhD, will use his grant to study synergistic treatment for Ewing sarcoma, a group of bone and soft-tissue cancers. Asada is investigating exploiting a DNA damage repair defect, resulting from EWS-FLI1 expression or loss of EWSR1 protein.

These awards also support the work of three early career researchers examining the behavior of brain gliomas, which are malignant brain tumors that come from glial cells in the brain or spinal cord. Gustavo Alencastro Veiga Cruzeiero, PhD, is researching compounds that block the spread and communication of high-grade glioma cells. His goal is to stop the growth and reduce the invasiveness of glioma subtype DHG-H3G34 mutant tumors. This study seeks to understand the biology of these tumors and revolutionize pediatric therapies. Timothy Chang, MD, PhD, is examining if senescence, a natural response to stress once thought to suppress tumors, contributes to the growth and radiation resistance of diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs). DMGs are an extremely aggressive form of brain tumors in children. Jenna Robinson, PhD, is researching pediatric brain cancers to uncover why the protein SMARCAL1 is important to the uncontrolled division of mutant cells in the BRAF gene. She is investigating if SMARCAL1 inhibition may be used to stop cancer growth.

By underwriting this innovative research, ALSF honors Alex Scott’s bravery—bringing hope to children with cancer and their families.

title: Freedlander bequest focuses on inflammatory breast cancer
body:
Spring 2026
By Kathy Clute

The estate of Ruth Freedlander made a $1.8 million bequest to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute that will advance research into inflammatory breast cancer (IBC), a rare and aggressive disease that is particularly difficult to treat.

With the bequest, Dana-Farber established the Freedlander Fund for Inflammatory Breast Cancer under the direction of Sara Tolaney, MD, MPH, chief of the Division of Breast Oncology. Freedlander made the gift in memory of her daughter, Lynn November of Westhampton, N.Y., who passed away from the disease. The gift also honors Freedlander’s parents, Else and Sigfried Oppenheimer.

“The bequest is a testament to Ruth’s respect for Dana-Farber and her tremendous love for her daughter, whom she wanted to be remembered,” said her friend Jean Rosensaft, director of the Heller Museum at Hebrew Union College in New York. “Ruth was so grateful for Dana-Farber’s great medical care, its research and innovation, and its ability to help Lynn.” Freedlander, of Teaneck, N.J., died in 2023 at age 92. She and her parents fled Nazi Germany to Antwerp, Belgium, when she was a child, and the family later found refuge in the United States.

Freedlander went on to become a successful stockbroker and investment advisor who served as a trustee and visionary for the Dr. Bernard Heller Foundation, which supports four Jewish educational institutions. “Ruth was an extraordinary woman who never forgot her childhood roots, her experience of persecution, discrimination, and escape from the Nazis, and then coming to this country and finding freedom and opportunity,” said Rosensaft. “She was spirited, she was determined, and she had very passionate ideas and feelings about everything that she did in her life.”

Freedlander’s bequest to Dana-Farber targets IBC, a form of invasive ductal carcinoma that accounts for only 1% to 5% of all breast cancers, according to the American Cancer Society. It often does not cause a lump and may not show up on a mammogram. Instead, breasts may become swollen and red because cancer cells are blocking lymph vessels in the skin, and it spreads and grows more quickly than other types of breast cancer. Thanks to Freedlander’s gift, Dana-Farber can continue making significant strides in IBC research and treatment. “The Freedlander Fund will be pivotal in advancing the understanding of the disease and developing more targeted therapies and improved patient outcomes,” said Tolaney. “Ruth and Lynn will be a constant source of inspiration as we strive to fulfill our mission of lessening the burden of cancer.”

title: CRI grants accelerate immunotherapy research at Dana-Farber
body:
Spring 2026
By Hannah White Hannah

The Cancer Research Institute (CRI) is advancing bold new strategies to harness the immune system against cancer through two grants at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. Nearly $1.5 million will support two exceptional investigators—Judith Agudo, PhD, and Samantha Fernandez, PhD,—whose innovative research is uncovering how cancer evades immune detection and how those defenses can be dismantled.

The CRI Lloyd J. Old STAR Program recognizes scientists whose outstanding and innovative research has had a major impact on the cancer field and has the potential to stimulate new directions in cancer immunology. With the STAR award, Agudo is tackling her proposal, Decoding Cancer Cell Plasticity as a Driver of Immune Evasion During Tumor Evolution. Her lab studies the small population of “stem-like” tumor cells that often survive treatment and cause relapse or metastasis. With this funding, Agudo and her team are developing advanced models that more closely reflect patient biology to uncover how these resilient cells adapt to immune pressure and persist despite treatment.

“For immunotherapies to succeed, we must understand the mechanisms that allow certain cancer cells to resist immune attack,” said Agudo. “This funding allows us to pursue that knowledge in new and dynamic ways—work that will ultimately help us design better, more durable therapies for patients.” The second CRI Irvington Postdoctoral Fellowship will provide $243,000 of support for Fernandez. Her proposal is called Discovering Conserved Mechanisms of Interferon Dependent Cancer Immunity Using Cross-Kingdom Interactions. Fernandez’s research explores the complex role of interferon signaling in cancer, investigating how evolutionary conserved mechanisms of anti-tumor immunity can both drive strong immune responses and, paradoxically, enable tumor cells to hide from the immune system. Insights from this work could inform future generations of immunotherapies. 

These projects exemplify the power of philanthropy to drive discovery. By supporting investigators like Agudo and Fernandez, CRI is helping Dana-Farber scientists pursue bold ideas that expand the frontiers of immunotherapy. This support empowers researchers to take risks, follow promising leads, and bring us closer to a future where immunotherapy benefits more patients worldwide.

title: IWMF awards $1.4 million to Dana-Farber investigators, fueling Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia research
body:
Spring 2026
By Hannah White Hannah

For more than two decades, the International Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia Foundation (IWMF) has been a vital philanthropic partner to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, accelerating research into Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinemia (WM), a rare, slow-growing blood cancer. Recently, the IWMF took a significant step in combating WM, awarding more than $1.4 million in grants to three Dana-Farber investigators. The funding will support groundbreaking studies that can lead to better understanding of disease biology, overcoming treatment resistance, and providing more personalized, effective therapies for people living with WM.

Dana-Farber’s Steven Treon, MD, PhD, is one grant recipient that stands to benefit from the IWMF’s support. Treon’s team previously helped uncover a key genetic change found in most people with Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinemia. That work paved the way for ibrutinib, a drug that has transformed care for many patients. As some cancers learn to evade ibrutinib, Treon’s new IWMF-funded project focuses on eliminating those escape routes, delivering options for patients who stop responding to ibrutinib, with a goal of accelerating the most promising therapies to clinical trials.

These grants highlight the [our] deep commitment to driving progress and turning advances in genetics and cell research into tangible treatment options.

Paul Kitchen, Chairman of the Board

Constantine Mitsiades, MD, PhD, received an IWMF grant to decode the “control room” inside WM cells—the proteins that turn genes on and off. These transcription factor teams tell cancer cells when to grow, survive, and resist treatment. Mitsiades will chart these networks in depth and test what happens when key switches are turned off. By pinpointing these switches, his team hopes to guide safer, smarter drug combinations that are more effective and less toxic than traditional chemotherapy—helping doctors provide the right therapy to their patients.

Additionally, Dana-Farber investigator Hao Sun, MD, PhD, received an IWMF grant to study how different “branches” of WM change over time during ibrutinib treatment and how the body’s immune system shifts in response. In an upcoming clinical trial, his team will track how the cancer and immune system adapt to each other—revealing why treatment may lose effectiveness over time. These insights could help doctors detect resistance sooner and develop therapies that keep the disease under control longer. “These grants highlight the International Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia Foundation’s deep commitment to driving progress and turning advances in genetics and cell research into tangible treatment options,” said Delora Senft, IWMF president and CEO. “We are honored to support Dana-Farber’s innovative research as we work together to develop more effective, personalized therapies for patients and their families.

title: Dana-Farber’s Boston half team sets new record
body:
Spring 2026
By Sofia Elbadawi
Photography by Bryce Vickmark

Sunday, November 9, marked the Boston Athletic Association’s (B.A.A.’s) annual Boston Half, a scenic 13.1-mile race through Franklin Park and the Emerald Necklace Park System. Runners from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s 2025 Boston Half team raised a record-breaking $1,099,874.08, the highest fundraising total in the team’s 23-year history, pushing the fundraising total to a cumulative total of $10,986,664.

The 2025 team also set a recruitment record, with 740 runners forming Dana-Farber’s largest Boston Half team yet. For many team members, running and fundraising on behalf of Dana-Farber was a way to thank care teams, honor loved ones, or even celebrate overcoming a cancer diagnosis. 

“After being diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia in June 2024, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and my wonderful stem cell donor gave me a second chance at a life with a transplant,” shared Lucy Hollis, a member of this 2025 team.

Lucy was motivated to run the 2025 Boston Half as a way to celebrate her recovery while giving back to Dana-Farber; “Raising funds for such a critical mission, defying cancer, is a way to say thank you to everyone who cared for me,” she said.

“For patients like me from Bermuda, or other places where local hospitals can’t offer the complex treatment required for certain cancers, Dana-Farber is an absolute lifeline. Knowing that their research into new, more effective treatments will benefit patients everywhere is huge,” Lucy added.

For others, like Tony Bougiouris, the race was a way to honor loved ones, and turn grief into purpose. 

Running the Boston half for Dana-Farber gave me a way to honor my sister’s memory, carry her spirit forward, and transform my grief into action by supporting research that saves lives.

Tony Bougiouris, a member of Dana-Farber’s 2025 Boston Half team

“I lost my sister, Maggie, to cancer last September—the day after her 47th birthday. Running the Boston Half for Dana-Farber Cancer Institute gave me a way to honor her memory, carry her spirit forward, and transform my grief into action by supporting research that saves lives,”  he said. When asked what kept him inspired during the months of training and fundraising, Tony said, “Watching Maggie face cancer with strength and grace motivated me to fundraise, advocate, and run for others still in the fight. Dana-Farber’s work gives hope to families like mine.”

Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund has partnered with the Boston Half since 2003 as the race’s presenting sponsor and exclusive charity team. Through this relationship, Dana-Farber runners have been able to raise millions to support groundbreaking cancer research and compassionate patient care. Looking ahead, Dana-Farber’s Boston Half team plans to continue the tradition of defying cancer, 13.1 miles at a time.

title: Expect Miracles Foundation invests $1.1 million to accelerate cancer breakthroughs at the Belfer Center
body:
Spring 2026
By Hannah White Hannah
Photography by Allie Joseph

For more than 25 years, Expect Miracles Foundation has united leaders across the financial services industry and beyond to advance life-saving cancer research and support those impacted by the disease. Now, with a generous $1.1 million gift to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s Robert and Renée Belfer Center for Applied Cancer Science, the Foundation is deepening its impact and helping to drive the next generation of targeted cancer therapies.

Founded on the belief that business leaders can be powerful agents of change, Expect Miracles Foundation raises funds through signature events including its East Coast and Atlantic Coast Classic golf tournaments, annual galas in Boston and New York City, a peer-to-peer Distance Challenge, and marathon teams across the country. Through these efforts—and the extraordinary generosity of the Expect Miracles community—the organization has raised more than $15 million cumulatively for Dana-Farber.

“We’re proud to partner with Dana-Farber’s Belfer Center to accelerate research that brings new treatments and hope to patients faster,” said Frank Strauss, founder and chairman of Expect Miracles Foundation. “This gift represents the commitment of thousands of individuals in our industry who believe in Dana-Farber’s mission and the importance of investing in innovation that saves lives.” The Belfer Center bridges the gap between scientific discovery and the development of new cancer therapies. Its researchers collaborate closely with pharmaceutical and biotechnology partners to translate promising laboratory findings into clinical advances for patients.

“Support from Expect Miracles Foundation enables us to pursue bold, high-impact research that might otherwise take years to reach patients,” said Pasi A. Jänne, MD, PhD, director of the Belfer Center and the David M. Livingston, MD, Chair at Dana-Farber. “Their generosity fuels discovery and collaboration—two essential ingredients for progress in the fight against cancer.” Expect Miracles Foundation’s dedication to defying cancer has earned them widespread recognition, including the 2025 Boston Red Sox Jimmy Fund Award for their outstanding commitment to Dana-Farber’s lifesaving mission. Their latest gift continues that tradition, emboldening their belief that with community, compassion, and perseverance, miracles aren’t just possible—they’re expected.

title: Crowley gift accelerates innovative research in chronic lymphocytic leukemia
body:
Spring 2026
By Michael Quinn
Photography by Sam Ogden

Brian and Jane Crowley are longtime supporters of Dana-Farber who made their first gift nearly two decades ago to advance melanoma research in memory of Brian’s sister. So, when Brian was later diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), he and Jane knew just where to go for care and how they could help improve the lives of other patients too.

Recently, the Crowleys made a generous gift to support the Jane and Brian Crowley Fund for CLL Research, which advances investigations led by Brian’s doctor, Jennifer Brown, MD, PhD, director of Dana-Farber’s Center for Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia and the Worthington and Margaret Collette Professor of Medicine in the Field of Hematologic Oncology at Harvard Medical School. Motivated by their appreciation for Brown’s care and trust in her expertise, they provided pivotal resources for her lab to use without restriction rather than tying it to a specific project. As a result, Brown is free to apply these funds where the opportunity and impact can be greatest, accelerating groundbreaking CLL research to uncover familial factors in disease onset and progression, explore ways to overcome treatment resistance, and develop next generation therapies that minimize side effects.

Brown’s lab has made significant strides in all three priority areas. For example, her team found that patients with inherited ATM mutations were more likely to have relatives with CLL, highlighting genetic risk and supporting more personalized monitoring and treatment.

Additionally, they published findings from a study showing that the longer CLL patients remain on targeted therapy, the more likely they are to develop specific genetic mutations leading to resistance. Other mechanisms seem to play a greater role in treatment relapse, an insight that may guide researchers in developing new ways to overcome it. Lastly, Brown’s team demonstrated the promise of a novel combination therapy with enhanced precision in attacking cancer cells, offering a safer and more effective option for patients with untreated CLL. These and other practice-changing advances have earned Brown widespread recognition for research excellence, including being named numerous times to the annual Highly Cited Researchers list of the Institute for Scientific Information at Clarivate, which identifies investigators who produced multiple papers ranking in the top 1% by citations for their discipline and year of publication. At the same time, she is renowned for her compassionate care as a clinician and has been repeatedly included on Boston magazine’s annual lists of “Top Doctors.” The Crowleys trust that Brown will make an even bigger impact with their gift, pursuing breakthroughs that benefit patients everywhere. “Dr. Brown is an accomplished leader in the lab and clinic,” said Brian. “We are honored to support her team and play a role in their progress.”

title: $1 million gift fuels survivorship and precision prostate cancer research at Dana-Farber
body:
Spring 2026
By Cyrena Musset
Photography by Jamie Phillips/Capehart Photography

As a child, Donald M. Ephraim, when asked what he wanted to be when he grew up, replied “a philanthropist.” The questioner was impressed with the nobility of the answer. But when asked why, he said that compared to his family’s modest circumstances, philanthropists seemed so wealthy. Because of those circumstances, he lived at home and paid his own way through college and law school, built a successful legal career, and in the early 1990s established a foundation. With three sons in college and, later, two in law school, the giving began modestly but steadily. Over time, he found deep satisfaction in directing support to organizations whose work measurably improves lives.

That conviction crystalized when he was diagnosed with prostate cancer. When he initially sought care at a major Chicago hospital, his experience was marked by delays and a lack of urgency and coordination. Fortunately, Don’s partner Terri Sriberg, whose late husband and daughter-in-law had both received care at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, knew just where to go next. She called her good friend, Judie Schlager, who had extensive ties with Dana-Farber, and who arranged the appointments. Dana-Farber’s medical team responded immediately by scheduling examinations with multiple specialists, arranging critical tests, and setting up a clear treatment plan.

Dana-Farber makes you feel safe. When we go there, we just know they’re going to find a solution to make things better.

Terri Sriberg

At Dana-Farber, Don encountered a culture that matches its expertise: from valet and reception to appointment clerks, testing staff, nurses, and physicians; everyone is upbeat, responsive, and compassionate—on the phone and in person. “From what we’ve heard, many cancer centers are much bigger and really overwhelming,” Terri said. “Dana-Farber makes you feel safe. When we go there, we just know they’re going to find a solution to make things better.” 

“My doctor, Alicia Morgans, is wonderful,” Don added, “She is a great caregiver, totally forthright and responsive. I am most appreciative of what she’s done for me and being able to help her continue some of her work is deeply rewarding.” 

Don’s philanthropy is focused on impact, which is why he recently gave $1 million to support the research of Alicia Morgans, MD, MPH, in prostate cancer and survivorship. Now at 94, he wants his legacy to remain impactful, helping future patients benefit from more targeted therapies with fewer side effects. Today’s testosterone-blocking approaches can lead to downstream effects; donor support helps investigators develop precision treatments that reduce reliance on broad hormone suppression while maintaining effectiveness. Philanthropy accelerates this work—funding trials, enabling collaboration, and sustaining the patient-centered services that make complex care navigable.

Don’s philanthropic message is clear: Dana-Farber’s combination of excellence and humanity is uncommon and worthy of supporting and amplifying. He has seen Dana-Farber solve problems and restore dignity, and he takes quiet pride in helping ensure that experience for a prostate cancer patient he will never meet. “If I can play even a small part in that,” he said, “I’m quite happy.”

title: Stephen B. Farber & Deirdre E. Curley make $1 million gift
body:
Spring 2026
By Hannah White Hannah

Steve is the son of Dr. Sidney Farber, who founded the Children’s Cancer Research Foundation (now Dana-Farber) in 1947 and is widely regarded as the father of modern chemotherapy. Steve joined the Board of Trustees in 1973 and is currently its longest serving member. For 52 years, Steve and Dee have strongly supported presidential initiatives, capital campaigns, endowed chairs, and other Dana-Farber priorities. 

Their professional lives have focused on public service. After completing studies at Harvard and Princeton, Steve worked to improve U.S. fiscal and intergovernmental policies and operations, starting with the new anti-poverty programs of the 1960s. He was an adviser to Indiana Congressman John Brademas, New Jersey Governor Richard J. Hughes, and Harvard University President Derek Bok.

We understand the value and importance of unrestricted gifts. The overriding goal is to maximize support of all kinds in order to build on Dana-Farber’s extraordinary achievements over the past three quarters of a century.

Steve Farber and Dee Curley

He then served as executive director of the National Governors’ Association; chairman of Concordia Group, a national advisory service on fiscal and intergovernmental affairs; and chief adviser for the County Council of Montgomery County, Maryland. Dee, a Wellesley College graduate, worked for the U.S. Bureau of Consumer Protection, the Massachusetts Council on Crime and Correction, and Wisconsin Governor Patrick J. Lucey as the state’s director of intergovernmental relations. She then served as the chief analyst for fiscal and trade issues at the National Governors’ Association, where she and Steve met, and as Assistant Director of the U.S. Trade and Development Agency. “My father lives on at Dana-Farber, just as he does in us,” Steve said. “This conviction is what animates the gifts Dee and I have made over the years. We are proud to support many vitally important organizations. Dana-Farber is and always will be foremost among them.”

Steve and Dee added: “While some of our past gifts have been for specific purposes, we understand the value and importance of unrestricted gifts. The overriding goal is to maximize support of all kinds in order to build on Dana-Farber’s extraordinary achievements over more than three quarters of a century.”

title: Conquer Cancer® grants target several types of cancer
body:
Spring 2026
By Kathy Clute

Conquer Cancer®, the ASCO Foundation, has fueled groundbreaking research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute for decades. Its most recent grantmaking directs $1.3 million in awards to seven early and midcareer physician-scientists tackling a wide range of challenges, including how to identify patients likely to develop high-risk prostate cancer and understanding how food insecurity affects survivors of childhood cancers.

Among the grants are prestigious multiyear Advanced Clinical Research Awards given to two assistant professors leading clinical trials of new treatments for two aggressive, hard-to-treat cancers. Filipa Lynce, MD, FASCO, is directing a phase 2 clinical study to determine whether a combination of two FDA-approved drugs will prove more effective than current presurgical treatments against stage III HER2-expressing inflammatory breast cancer (IBC).

“IBC is a rare but aggressive form of breast cancer that spreads quickly and is responsible for up to 10% of breast cancer related deaths,” said Lynce. “Unfortunately, there are no specific treatments for it, and standard therapies are associated with worse outcomes compared to other types of breast cancer.”

Early research suggests that the drugs she is testing—an antibody-drug conjugate combined with an immunotherapy agent—may work well together, and her clinical trial will evaluate whether the combination therapy is safe and effective. 

Elizabeth Stover, MD, PhD, is investigating advanced-stage ovarian cancer, which is typically treated with surgery and platinum-based chemotherapy but usually becomes resistant and recurs. Her new clinical trial targets recurrent disease that is resistant to platinum.

“We are studying whether we can add a new drug to a standard chemotherapy drug, paclitaxel, to enhance the killing of platinum-resistant ovarian cancer cells,” Stover said. Laboratory studies indicate that combining a drug that degrades a specific protein called BCL-XL with paclitaxel could prove more effective than the chemotherapy alone; this is the first time the combination is being evaluated in patients.

Fellows Jordan Chinai, MD, PhD, and Dan Gui, MD, PhD, both focused on pancreatic cancer; and Nathalie Javidi-Sharifi, MD, PhD (Richter’s Transformation in chronic lymphocytic leukemia), received Young Investigator Awards, as did Instructor Jeremiah Wala, MD, PhD (prostate cancer). Rahela Aziz-Bose, MD, was given a Career Development Award (food insecurity in survivors of childhood cancer). 

Conquer Cancer is committed to investing in the future of cancer research and discovery. By providing critical support to researchers at every career stage—including those working at institutions like Dana-Farber—the foundation empowers them to tackle the most complex challenges facing people with cancer. This essential funding allows physician scientists to turn innovative ideas into real-world breakthroughs that deliver vital improvements and save lives.

title: Zakim Center turns 25: Donor generosity continues to fuel integrative therapies
body:
Spring 2026
By Kathy Clute
Photography by John Deputy

When the late Leonard “Lenny” Zakim was being treated for multiple myeloma in the 1990s, he found that complementary therapies such as acupuncture, massage, and Tai Chi eased the side effects of chemotherapy and radiation. But accessing those modalities was difficult, and he dreamed of—and lobbied for—a space at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute where they could be provided to other patients.

In 2000, largely thanks to Zakim’s persistence, Dana-Farber established the Leonard P. Zakim Center for Integrative Therapies and Healthy Living. It started small, as one room off the Dana Building lobby. Now it has grown into a spacious hub of clinical services, group programs, and transformative research that celebrated its 25th anniversary in October 2025. The Zakim Center serves thousands of patients every month—in person and online—and conducts peer-reviewed research on how integrative therapies mitigate the side effects of treatment and improve patient outcomes.

“Lenny Zakim came to the leadership of Dana-Farber saying, ‘We want a center that’s not focused on finding new chemotherapy agents, but on helping people feel better by incorporating treatments that have been available for millennia,’” Jennifer Ligibel, MD, director of the Zakim Center, told attendees at the anniversary celebration. “It was a radical concept, but very much in line with Dana-Farber’s long-term mission of not just treating the cancer, but treating the patient and family. And over time, as the number of patients that we treated grew, our footprint did as well, transforming into a beautiful center designed to be an oasis for patients going through the tumult of a cancer journey.”

Unlike conventional cancer treatments, health insurance doesn’t cover many complementary therapies. Yet thanks to millions of dollars in donations since 2000, most of the Zakim Center’s offerings are free. “We wouldn’t be able to do what we do for our patients without our partnership with our amazing donors,” Ligibel said. 

In addition to integrative practices such as acupuncture, massage, Tai Chi, meditation, expressive arts therapies, and Qigong, the Zakim Center also offers a full portfolio of healthy living programs. These include exercise classes, strength training, one-on-one health coaching sessions, nutrition seminars, cooking demonstrations, and weight-management programs. Through the My Zakim online portal, patients and families can also access many of these programs virtually. The platform has logged over 1.2 million worldwide visits since 2020, including more than 310,000 in 2025.

title: Celebrating our community fundraising heroes
body:
Spring 2026
By Sofia Elbadawi

At the heart of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund’s mission to defy cancer is a community making a difference–one dollar, one event, and one story at a time.  Together, these community fundraising heroes organize events of all types and sizes, raising more than $6.5 million annually. This spring, we’re spotlighting a few of those who are defying cancer in their communities and turning passion into purpose.

The Dustin Strong 5K

Amine Bentahar, a young swimmer from Massachusetts, was shocked to find out his friend and fellow swim-teammate, Dustin, had been diagnosed with leukemia. Determined to help, Amine reached out to Dustin’s father. Together, they planned the Dustin Strong 5K, a fundraiser that would galvanize friends, family, and strangers alike to raise money for Dana-Farber.

At the inaugural event, a huge turnout from the community helped exceed all expectations. “Creating a fundraiser in honor of Dustin was a way to turn a very negative situation into something positive—something to bring the community together,” Amine said. 

Today, Dustin is cancer-free, and the mission of the Dustin Strong 5K lives on through the Dustin Strong organization, which continues to host fundraisers to support and honor other young patients fighting cancer.

Coding for Cancer

Self-proclaimed “nerd,” Sherry Knotek, taught technology and STEM classes at St. Clement’s Regional Catholic School in Saratoga Springs, New York. Sherry found Dana-Farber after receiving a shocking neuroendocrine cancer diagnosis in 2021. When she met with Dana-Farber oncologist Matt Yurgelun, MD, Sherry’s fear turned into optimism—“The knowledge he had and the treatment options available for my cancer were incredible.”

As a teacher, Sherry knows young people can support the fight against cancer by turning a passion, like coding, into purpose. She also wanted to teach her students how important technology, and other STEM subjects, are to cancer research. That’s why she decided to host an event called “Coding for Cancer.” The event included Sherry’s past and present students, with participants building their own fundraising sites and coding in teams. Coding for Cancer successfully raised thousands for Dana-Farber, and offered comfort to Sherry, who was overwhelmed by how many students, teachers, parents, and friends participated. Though Sherry is now retired, her legacy of supporting Dana-Farber’s mission to defy cancer continues with the yearly Coding for Cancer event.

Gaming for Good

When Massachusetts native “Wabba”—as he is known in the gamer community—became passionate about video games as a kid, he never imagined his hobby would one day help cancer patients. Wabba, who prefers to go by his gaming moniker, represents one-third of the podcast “Three Dads and a Console,” formed with two of his friends from the gaming community. The three dads are ambassadors for Outright Games, a family-friendly video game publisher.

In addition to sneak peeks of upcoming games, Outright also allows them to support Dana-Farber and the Jimmy Fund. After hosting some fundraising livestreams, Wabba and his friends began partnering with Outright to support patients directly. For every $250 their podcast raised for Dana-Farber and the Jimmy Fund, Outright agreed to donate some of their most popular games to the Jimmy Fund Clinic at Dana-Farber. Wabba hoped sharing these games might offer patients a welcome distraction. “If it helps patients or their families, then it’s one of the most valuable uses of my time,” he said.

title: Philanthropic support advances faculty work
body:
Spring 2026
By Caitlin Roberts
Photography by Sam Ogden

Each day at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, faculty members work toward research breakthroughs, provide care and moments of hope to patients, and strive to go above and beyond in the fight against cancer.

Jenny Mack, MD, MPH, faculty vice president for the Office of Faculty Development (OFD) and professor of pediatrics, sees it every day in her role—and has experienced it as a long-time faculty member.

“Whether they are caring for patients or conducting research that can change the face of cancer care, there are so many ways that faculty members help shape the endeavors of Dana-Farber,” shared Mack. “Our donors see that and understand that investing in our faculty means investing in Dana-Farber.”

Philanthropic support helps propel this work forward. Created in 2008, the OFD strives to support career development, build community, aid faculty members during critical moments in their personal lives, and ensure that Dana-Farber is a place they can thrive. Thanks to continuous support totaling more than $2 million, the OFD has provided awards to faculty members across Dana-Farber in a variety of disciplines. This generosity ensures that faculty can deliver the best in research and care for patients, while also flourishing at Dana-Farber, especially those beginning their careers. In fact, many who were supported early in their careers hold leadership positions at Dana-Farber today.

“Supporting early career faculty members can help them for many years, creating avenues to access grants, launch projects, and providing them opportunities that can be more difficult to come by early in their careers. This support can have a ripple effect for faculty members as they move forward, creating long-term success,” said Mack. Generosity toward the OFD helps aid in patient care, too. “By supporting the OFD, donors are supporting the great things faculty members do, including doing their best for patients, both here at Dana-Farber and around the world as scientific discoveries are disseminated across the globe,” commented Mack.

title: Dana-Farber’s Future Cancer Hospital
body:
Spring 2026

Last March 2025, the Massachusetts Public Health Council voted unanimously to approve a Determination of Need (DON) for Dana-Farber Cancer Institute to build a 300-bed cancer hospital in the Longwood Medical Area. This approval was a key milestone in the regulatory process that will enable Dana-Farber to build a visionary new inpatient facility that will redefine how cancer is treated.

Dana-Farber is renowned for its revolutionary, groundbreaking research and expert, highly specialized patient care. The hospital will function as the primary connector at the center of the clinical collaboration between Dana-Farber, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), and Harvard Medical Faculty Physicians (HMFP). It will be the only hospital of its kind in the region. The future cancer hospital has a community of supporters that is building momentum—fueling this next chapter of innovative treatment and care for patients and families. More stories of their commitment to our bold vision for the future of cancer care will be featured in future issues of Impact.

title: From the Chief Philanthropy Officer
body:
Spring 2026

Dear Friends,

As the year unfolds and progress accelerates, I am grateful for the passion and generosity of our donor community. Together, we have built tremendous momentum and are transforming cancer research and care. Your continued belief in Dana-Farber’s mission is laying the foundation for the future cancer hospital, a once-in-a-generation effort to expand world-class care and accelerate discovery for the patients and families who count on us.

Dana-Farber’s unique 50-50 model—equal commitment to cancer research and patient care—powers a virtuous cycle: breakthroughs in the lab rapidly inform clinical care and insights from the clinic spark new scientific questions. This integrated approach isn’t just a philosophy; it is a proven engine for progress.

Our commitment to research is unwavering—and growing. The future cancer hospital will strengthen our 50-50 model by creating more opportunities for collaboration, expanding access to clinical trials, and elevating the standard of care for every patient. Philanthropic leaders are providing targeted support for the future cancer hospital, enabling us to sustain and expand strategic research initiatives. This proactive approach deepens discovery, expands clinical care through a clear growth plan, and engages a broader community of supporters to amplify impact.

A landmark grant from the Elaine and Eduardo Saverin Foundation, featured in this issue, exemplifies continued investment in the bench-to-bedside-to-bench continuum in metastatic breast cancer. Their commitment will accelerate clinical trials, sharpen data and liquid biopsy insights, and apply AI to personalize care and anticipate resistance, so that the right therapies reach patients faster.

Because of the Elaine and Eduardo Saverin Foundation and a community of donors that span the globe, we are strengthening the ecosystem that has made and will continue to make Dana-Farber distinct—where science and care continuously inform each other, and where every gift brings us closer to a world free from the burden of cancer. Thank you for believing in this vision and for helping us build a better future for every patient. 

With heartfelt appreciation,

Melany N. Duval
Senior Vice President and Chief Philanthropy Officer

title: Pan-Mass Challenge makes record-breaking $78 million gift to drive Dana-Farber’s progress against cancer
body:
Winter 2025
By Michael Quinn
Photography by Pan-Mass Challenge

The Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), a bike-a-thon that raises more money for charity than any other single athletic fundraising event in the world, has built an unparalleled track record for success strengthened by touchstone traditions and continuous improvements in pursuit of the goal of defying cancer.

Anchored in its storied past and animated by its hopeful future, the PMC made a record-breaking gift of $78 million to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, bringing the organization’s cumulative total to an astounding $1.125 billion raised since 1980. Powering this milestone contribution was the 46th annual PMC ride on Aug. 2-3, when 6,500 riders from 12 countries and 47 states pedaled 14 routes across Massachusetts. They were aided by 3,500 volunteers and 200 corporate sponsors, whose support ensured that 100% of every rider-raised dollar went directly to cancer research and care at Dana-Farber for the 19th consecutive year. 1,100 riders and volunteers were cancer survivors or current patients, considered Living Proof® of the PMC mission. Additionally, 160 Dana-Farber employees volunteered or rode, in some cases to fundraise for their own cancer research.

As Dana-Farber’s largest single contributor, representing 67% of the Jimmy Fund’s annual revenue, the PMC drives everything at Dana-Farber, accelerating breakthrough research to maximize innovation and progress while elevating essential care programs that support patients from diagnosis through survivorship. According to Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD, President and CEO at Dana-Farber and the Richard and Susan Smith Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, the PMC’s effect on Dana-Farber and its work is palpable and powerful. “Each day, we witness the profound impact of PMC funding,” he said, “We see it in new lifesaving treatments, in the determination of our researchers to make transformative discoveries, and in the ever-improving outcomes of our patients.”

“We ride to ensure that hope is never extinguished.”

Billy Starr, founder and chairman of the PMC, and Dana-Farber Trustee

A seven-year PMC rider, Ebert began his two-day trek at the Sturbridge Host Hotel, as have thousands of participants since 1981. 2025 marked Sturbridge’s final year as the PMC’s central Massachusetts starting line, which will move to the College of the Holy Cross in Worcester in 2026 to accommodate more participants, promote further growth, and provide more accessible and modern facilities. Susan Brogan, longtime Sturbridge coordinator with Matt McGuiness, reflected on the town’s indelible place in PMC history and Worcester’s potential to further elevate the ride. “Sturbridge really embraced the PMC, and what started here has impacted cancer worldwide,” said Brogan. “Our aim is to keep the needle moving forward, and Worcester provides an ideal opportunity for that.”

Billy Starr, founder and chairman of the PMC and a Dana-Farber Trustee, celebrated Sturbridge as “a cherished chapter in the PMC story” and underscored the importance of everyone’s continued commitment amid economic uncertainty and unprecedented cuts in federal research funding. “When others pull back this community accelerates,” Starr said. “We ride not just to raise money, but to support breakthroughs, ensure that hope is never extinguished, and make absolutely certain that nothing stands in the way of the cures we aspire to fund together.”

title: Fostering patient-centered research
body:
Winter 2025
By Kathy Clute
Photography by Sam Ogden

How can exercise and diet improve the cognitive and physical abilities of cancer survivors 65 and older? Can artificial intelligence tools analyze clinical notes and other data in electronic medical records to determine which treatments are most effective?

Christina Dieli-Conwright, PhD, MPH, is a clinical exercise physiologist and the principal investigator (PI) in a 5-year collaboration with the University of Miami to determine whether older cancer survivors and their support persons can improve their cognitive and physical functioning through targeted lifestyle interventions.

Dieli-Conwright and her team are offering supervised and unsupervised home-based exercise and diet programs to 764 older cancer survivors and their primary caregivers, who are most often spouses or other family members. The participants are 65 or older and racially and ethnically diverse. One group will receive “gold standard” virtual aerobic and resistance exercise led by a certified trainer as well as virtual coaching by a registered dietician to promote adherence to a healthy Mediterranean diet that emphasizes fruits and vegetables, unsaturated fats, and less processed food.

The second group will be given the same diet recommendations and exercise intervention and equipment but will not receive the virtual coaching.

“There will be more than 26.1 million cancer survivors by 2040, and three quarters of them will be 65 or older—many with treatment-related side effects that affect their physical and cognitive functioning,” said Dieli-Conwright. “We also know that support persons tend to be less healthy than their peers who do not have caregiving responsibilities. We want to see which intervention we are testing is most successful in promoting a better quality of life for both populations.”

Kenneth Kehl, MD, MPH, is a thoracic oncologist and a researcher in Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s Division of Population Sciences. He is PI on a project to improve outcomes for patients by developing machine-learning techniques to extract data on disease progression, treatments, and outcomes from the electronic health records (EHRs) of more than 150,000 patients with advanced cancer. “This will make it possible to compare treatments that may be widely deployed but that don’t attract the resources necessary for randomized controlled trials,” said Kehl.

Both studies are supported by funding from the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute, a nonprofit organization with a mission to fund research designed to provide patients, caregivers, and clinicians with the evidence-based information they need to make better-informed health and health care decisions.

  • Created an AI model to predict gene expression across human cells, advancing precision medicine. 
  • Introduced nursing-led research during Scholarship Week. 
  • Launched a first-of-its-kind lung cancer screening trial for never-smokers using a novel blood test. 
  • National Bureau of Economic Research reported that Dana-Farber has the highest scientific output per researcher of any institution in the world. 
  • Co-founded IGNITE, a first-ever consortium to eliminate health inequities in pediatric cancer care. 
  • Co-led a study of prostate cancer genetics in African populations to expand research in diverse groups. 
  • Advanced plans for a new cancer hospital through a bold clinical collaboration with BIDMC and HMFP. 
  • Opened a national-first simulation center to train oncology nurses in advanced ambulatory cancer care. 
  • Ranked among the best in pediatric cancer care nationally for the 18th straight year.

title: Jimmy Fund Radio-Telethon breaks records with $5.7 million raised for Dana-Farber
photo_credit: Photography by John Deputy, Matt Teuten
body:
Winter 2025
By Robbie Merritt and Nathalie Sczublewski
Photography by John Deputy, Matt Teuten

The WEEI/NESN Jimmy Fund Radio-Telethon presented by Arbella Insurance continued to be a beacon of support for Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund in August with a record-breaking fundraising year. The inspirational two-day event, which has united our community since 2002, raised more than $5.7 million, bringing its lifetime total to $80 million in support of adult and pediatric cancer care and research at Dana-Farber.

The broadcast went live from Fenway Park Aug. 18 and 19 from 6 a.m. through midnight and featured stories of resilience and hope from patients, doctors, community leaders, and special guests. This year’s event made history, surpassing $5 million for the first time thanks to gifts from more than 15,000 donors across all 50 states. More than 70% of donations were under $100, showcasing the collective impact of grassroots generosity. A transformative $1 million match from longtime Dana-Farber supporters and philanthropists Rob and Karen Hale further inspired donors to make a difference.

The event included special appearances from Jimmy Fund Co-Chairs Tom Caron and Brock Holt; Jimmy Fund Captain and Red Sox pitcher Garrett Whitlock; Brianna Wakefield, daughter of the late Tim and Stacy Wakefield; Red Sox manager Alex Cora; Boston Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla; and Boston Bruins head coach Marco Sturm, among many others. Gayle O’Connell, executive vice president and chief marketing officer of Arbella Insurance, also appeared on the broadcast, reflecting on the longstanding partnership between Arbella and the Jimmy Fund and their decades of supporting the annual event.

“We’re thrilled to have raised a record-breaking $5.7 million to support adults and children with cancer,” said Jimmy Fund Co-Chairs Tom Caron and Brock Holt. “Together, we have made history, making a significant impact in the fight against cancer, and with continued support, we can lessen the burden of cancer for families. We are humbled and grateful for the tremendous outpouring of support from Red Sox Nation during the WEEI/NESN Jimmy Fund Radio-Telethon presented by Arbella Insurance.”

title: American Cancer Society grants propel research and programs forward
body:
Winter 2025
By Cait Roberts

The American Cancer Society (ACS) recently awarded more than $3.1 million in grants to 11 Dana-Farber Cancer Institute investigators. These grants support various areas across Dana-Farber, including research on improved outcomes and patient assistance programming to help with access to care.

Supporting the next generation of researchers at Dana-Farber, Jennifer Mack, MD, MPH, received an institutional grant to develop a program for investigators to apply for seed grants, with three individuals funded annually to pursue their research.

A grant to support the work of Ann Partridge, MD, MPH, the Eric P. Winer, MD, Chair in Breast Cancer Research at Dana-Farber, will further her research into the treatment and care of adolescents and young adults with breast cancer who are more likely to suffer physically and emotionally after a diagnosis, compared with older patients. Partridge’s work aims to improve treatment outcomes and support quality of life for this population, as well as extend her impactful work to people with other types of young-onset breast cancer.

Focusing on treatments, Nilay Sethi, MD, PhD, was awarded a grant to aid in the development of new treatments that target the unique biology of colorectal cancer through a deeper review of factors related to the cancer’s shape-shifting behavior. Pere Puigserver, PhD, received a grant to help develop new strategies to enhance the efficacy of immunotherapeutic treatments for better patient outcomes.

The goal of grants received by Deborah Toffler, MSW, LCSW, and Christopher Lathan, MD, MS, MPH, the Christopher and Constance Hadley Family Chair at Dana-Farber, will help ensure Dana-Farber is accessible to all patients and families. Toffler’s grant will provide need-based lodging support to patients. Lathan’s grant will support Dana-Farber’s Community-Focused Patient Navigators to provide transportation for underserved patients.

“These scientists are on track to advance innovative cancer treatment, support, and care. We are excited to be a part of moving this work forward to help save lives.”

Christina Annunziata, MD, PhD, American Cancer Society

Building upon successful research on how to preserve healthy cells during cancer treatment, Olasunkanmi Olaoye, PhD, received funding to investigate a protein found to activate drugs specifically in tumors, helping to create safer treatments for patients.

Bringing comfort to patients, families, and Jimmy Fund Clinic team members is the professional responsibility of Opry, Dana-Farber’s first facility dog. Kate Nixon, CCLS, received a grant to support Opry’s work and efforts to provide tailored interventions for patients.

Other recent awardees include Yixiang Li, PhD; Sangwoo Park, PhD; and Sehyun Oh, PhD.

“The American Cancer Society is very proud to help fund these researchers and these critical areas of study,” said Christina Annunziata, MD, PhD, senior vice president, extramural discovery science at ACS. “These scientists are on track to advance innovative cancer treatment, support, and care. We are excited to be a part of moving this work forward to help save lives.”

title: Deitch’s formula for impact accelerates progress
body:
Winter 2025
By Amber Sinicrope
Photography by Celia D. Luna

Joseph S. Deitch, founder and Chairman Emeritus of Commonwealth Financial Network and creator of the Elevate Prize Foundation, is a philanthropist with a bold vision: to amplify changemakers and inspire collective action. He believes that empowering leaders in their fields can spark transformative change and redefine what’s possible.

Deitch’s recent $3 million gift to endow the Joseph Deitch Family Chair at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute exemplifies this vision. The chair, held by Eric Fischer, PhD, Director of the Chemical Biology Program at Dana-Farber, provides critical resources to fuel innovative cancer research. The decision to endow the chair was driven by Deitch’s trust in Dana-Farber’s leadership and his relationship with Laurie H. Glimcher, MD, President and CEO Emerita of Dana-Farber. “When Laurie told me this was one of her top priorities, that was enough for me,” Deitch recalled. “Then I met Eric. His brilliance, curiosity, and ability to unite diverse scientific disciplines made a powerful impression.”

Fischer’s pioneering work in targeted protein degradation—a therapeutic approach with wide-reaching potential—has positioned him as a leader in cancer biology. His research is reshaping drug development and transforming standards of care, offering promising alternatives to chemotherapy. Being named the inaugural incumbent of the Joseph Deitch Family Chair is an honor and a transformative opportunity for Fischer. “This recognition is not just for me, but for my entire lab and everyone who has contributed for more than a decade,” he said. “It’s also a vote of confidence in the future.”

The nature of the funding is especially critical, enabling Fischer and his team to take risks, test bold ideas, and unlock new directions. “Every dollar of flexible support can be multiplied tenfold in additional support,” Fischer reflected. “It accelerates everything—our speed, our reach, and ultimately, our impact on patients.”

“Philanthropy is deeply personal—find what speaks to you and act on it.”

Joseph S. Deitch

This remarkable gift builds on the $3 million Deitch contributed in 2023 to help launch the Centers for Early Detection and Interception and advance Dana-Farber’s Presidential Initiatives Fund. Deitch’s philanthropy also extends beyond Dana-Farber and cancer research. Through the Elevate Prize Foundation, he supports changemakers across disciplines while also empowering communities to create local solutions to global challenges.

Deitch’s giving centers on finding proven leaders with the vision and capacity to drive change—investing in their growth and amplifying their work to draw greater support. “I’m not someone who seeks the spotlight,” he said. “But I hope endowing this chair inspires others to think about how they can make a difference. Philanthropy is deeply personal—find what speaks to you and act on it.”

title: Family of Jane Rodgers honors her memory with new Dana-Farber chair
body:
Winter 2025
By Brittany Flaherty
Photography by Matt Teuten

When Jane Rodgers was diagnosed with cancer in 2019, her family took comfort in the fact that she was receiving the best possible care at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. Jane’s natural ability to connect with people meant her doctors and nurses soon felt like an extension of the family.

“My mom was the kind of person everyone loved,” said Jane’s daughter, Ariana Rodgers. “She radiated kindness and warmth. She was creative and intelligent. She loved painting watercolors and quilting and listening to college lectures on quantum mechanics just for fun.”

After Jane passed away in 2020, her family knew they wanted to make a gift together in her honor to demonstrate their gratitude for her care and to help prevent other patients and families from experiencing such a devastating loss. Their $3 million gift established the Jane Rodgers Chair at Dana-Farber with David A. Barbie, MD, director of the Lowe Center for Thoracic Oncology, as the first incumbent. “Philanthropy was really important to my mom,” said Ariana. “She emphasized that to us throughout her life and really cared about medical research. She would be very proud of this gift that we’re making and excited for the future of this research.”

Jane’s five children—Ariana, Brooke Eanes, Jack Bishop, Joyce-Ann Bishop, and Virginia Ermentrout—came together to make this special gift alongside Jane’s husband, Ronald Rodgers, through the MacDonald Family Foundation. The Jane Rodgers Chair will enable Barbie to further his thoracic oncology and immunotherapy research in perpetuity, with the goal of transforming care for patients with this challenging disease.

“I am truly honored by the incredibly generous support of the Jane Rodgers Family to carry on her legacy as we work to transform care for patients with lung cancer,” said Barbie. “This support will speed our efforts to expand treatment options, and we are grateful for the family’s meaningful partnership.”

Barbie is widely recognized for his pioneering work in the field of lung cancer, having led groundbreaking translational research that has expanded treatment options for patients, including those with KRAS-driven cancers previously considered undruggable. Ariana noted that persistent stigmas around lung cancer mean it doesn’t attract as much research support as other, less deadly diseases. Learning this confirmed her family’s decision to honor their mother’s memory and the compassionate team that had given her their time and care.

“The doctors are what set Dana-Farber apart. They’re passionate, knowledgeable, and we always felt heard and supported,” said Ariana, sharing that one of her mother’s nurses went out of her way to find her mom her favorite drink: Mexican Coca-Cola in a glass bottle. “It made my mom’s day, that special touch. Dana-Farber is incredible.”

title: Advancing Parkinson’s research: Spiegelman’s groundbreaking work
body:
Winter 2025
By Hannah White Hannah
Photography by Sam Ogden

From a remarkable act of generosity, the Tyler Family has donated $3 million to establish the Tyler Family Fund for Parkinson’s Research, supporting the groundbreaking work of Bruce Spiegelman, PhD, the Stanley J. Korsmeyer, MD, Professor of Cell Biology and Medicine at Harvard Medical School. This gift is a testament to their commitment to advancing research that could change the lives of millions affected by Parkinson’s Disease (PD), a condition that has personally impacted their family.

Spiegelman, a renowned leader in cancer biology and metabolism, has dedicated his career to exploring the molecular mechanisms underlying various diseases. His research, while primarily focused on cancer, often yields insights into other human diseases, including PD. Spiegelman’s innovative approach to understanding the molecular benefits of exercise has led to significant discoveries, particularly the identification of irisin, a protein with very significant therapeutic potential.

“Exercise and other forms of physical activity have been shown to markedly lower the incidence of PD and slow its progression,” Spiegelman explained. “Our goal is not to replace exercise but to use it as a platform for discovering new molecules that can be used as therapeutics for PD.”

Spiegelman’s lab was the first in the world to identify irisin, a protein linked to exercise, in 2012. Since then, they have demonstrated its striking effects in cellular and animal models of Alzheimer’s Disease and Parkinson’s Disease. In PD, the accumulation of toxic proteins like α-synuclein in neurons leads to motor symptoms. Irisin has shown promise in blocking this accumulation and preserving motor function in animal models.

“We are optimistic about the impact this research could have on stopping and perhaps reversing disease symptoms.”

Bruce Spiegelman, PhD

The Tyler Family Fund will enable Dr. Spiegelman’s team to accelerate their research, focusing on engineering irisin for therapeutic use. “This funding is absolutely crucial,” Spiegelman said. “It allows us to advance the study of irisin toward clinical trials, potentially offering a breakthrough treatment for PD. We are optimistic about the impact this research could have on stopping and perhaps even reversing disease symptoms.”

The Tyler Family’s gift offers new hope for those affected by PD. By supporting Spiegelman’s pioneering work, they are investing in a future where the disease and perhaps other neurological disorders can be effectively managed, and potentially even reversed. Their generosity underscores the importance of funding exploratory research that holds the promise of transformative breakthroughs.

title: Dolores Tassinari’s gift supports Hodgkin lymphoma care and research
body:
Winter 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

When Dolores Tassinari passed away at the age of 94 last year, she left behind a legacy of quiet strength, family devotion, and enduring generosity. A longtime resident of Plymouth, Mass., Dolores lived a life rooted in service—to her family, her community, and, in her final wishes, to a cause deeply personal to her heart.

In 2025, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute received an extraordinary estate gift of $2,464,652 from the Dolores E. Tassinari estate. Designated to support research and treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma, the gift honors the memory of Dolores’ beloved daughter, Suzanne Tassinari, who died of the illness in 1991.

For over four decades, Dolores worked alongside her husband, Ernest, as a public accountant in Plymouth. She was a woman of many passions, finding joy in gardening, reading, and cheering on the Red Sox. Dolores cherished weekly Scrabble games with her neighbors and took pride in her role as a mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother.

Her generous bequest to Dana-Farber reflects her enduring love for Suzanne and her desire to help others facing a similar diagnosis. It will help accelerate the work of Dana-Farber’s clinicians and scientists as they pursue new therapies and improved outcomes for patients with Hodgkin lymphoma.

“My parents understood that Dana-Farber was the institution with the deepest and broadest set of skills and experience in New England for cancer treatment and research.”

Mark Tassinari

Dolores’ legacy centers around her children, and she is survived by her daughter Marie Bower of Maryland, sons Edward Tassinari of Plymouth, and Mark Tassinari of Pembroke, New Hampshire—as well as five grandchildren and six great-grandchildren. Her gift ensures that her family’s story will continue to touch the lives of countless others.

“My parents understood that Dana-Farber was the institution with the deepest and broadest set of skills and experience in New England for cancer treatment and research,” said Mark.

“My sister’s condition ultimately proved incurable with the medical resources and treatments available in 1990 and 1991. It was my mother’s wish, and indeed that of our entire family, to contribute to the ongoing efforts at Dana-Farber to find new and effective treatments for the benefit of others.”

Dolores’ legacy, like the garden she so lovingly tended, will continue to grow—bringing hope to patients and families for generations to come.
