title: Suprenant’s intuitive philanthropy drives holistic cancer care
body:
Winter 2025
By Lucy McDonald

Cynthia Suprenant believes in keeping things simple. While her cumulative $1 million in contributions across Dana-Farber Cancer Institute may seem driven by results or carefully calculated outcomes, she insists her approach is rooted in something far more intuitive. Much like an investor backing promising startups, Suprenant places her trust in the leadership and vision of the institutions she supports, believing they are best equipped to identify where resources can make the greatest impact.

Suprenant traces her philosophy of giving back to her childhood, inspired by her Grandma Sullivan, who would carefully budget her household expenses and still set aside small amounts to give back to the local church. That early example of quiet generosity left a lasting impression on Suprenant, shaping her approach to philanthropy as an act of planting seeds and trusting experts to nurture them into something extraordinary. “I trust that the Institute will tell me what it needs,” Suprenant explained. “I just want to help smart people do things for sick people. I don’t want anything back from Dana-Farber other than for the good work to continue.” It was this same spirit of giving that guided her to Dana-Farber in 2017.

In addition to supporting Dana-Farber’s Institute priorities through unrestricted funding, Suprenant has focused her philanthropy on two key areas: the Program for Older Adults with Breast Cancer and the Leonard P. Zakim Center for Integrative Therapies and Healthy Living. Both reflect her intuitive approach to philanthropy, addressing needs that may not always be central to traditional cancer care but are deeply impactful for patients.

“I just want to help smart people do things for sick people.”

Cynthia Suprenant

The Program for Older Adults with Breast Cancer, one of the first of its kind in the U.S., serves patients over 70 by addressing their unique concerns. It offers specialized care, nutritional support, social workers, financial assistance, and integrative therapies. This multidisciplinary approach ensures patients receive holistic care to improve their quality of life. “A 78-year-old’s experience with recurrence is completely different from a 47-year-old’s,” Suprenant said. Her support has helped expand personalized care, empowering older patients with their treatment options.

The Leonard P. Zakim Center for Integrative Therapies and Healthy Living offerings align with Suprenant’s belief in holistic care. For 25 years, the center has complemented medical treatment with therapies that reduce pain, anxiety, and side effects while improving quality of life. With support from donors like Suprenant, the center has expanded its offerings, helping patients navigate their cancer journeys.

Through $1 million in contributions, Suprenant has shown philanthropy doesn’t need a formula. Guided by intuition and trust, her giving supports meaningful care, whether for older adults with breast cancer or integrative therapies and highlights the impact of thoughtful, heartfelt philanthropy.

title: Kicks for Cancer harnesses power of community to drive cancer research
body:
Winter 2025
By Caitlin Henault
Photography by Henry Morgan

Nearly 20 years ago, Concord-Carlisle High School hosted its first Kicks for Cancer soccer match to honor the memory of Lois Wells, the mother of assistant men’s soccer coach Steve Wells, who passed away from ovarian cancer. Today, Kicks for Cancer has grown into a vibrant week-long celebration that unites the community in a shared mission to honor loved ones impacted by cancer while supporting groundbreaking cancer research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

Anchored by its signature soccer tournament, which features 16 back-to-back matches between teams from surrounding towns in a single day, Kicks for Cancer has expanded to include a variety of sports, arts, and music, creating opportunities for all students to take part. In 2024, Kicks for Cancer reached a significant milestone, raising over $1 million to support Dana-Farber.

“Nearly everyone in our community can tell a story about someone in their life who has been affected by cancer,” said Trish Siefer, Kicks for Cancer’s event chair. “Kicks for Cancer unifies Concord-Carlisle—it gives us all a chance to honor survivors, remember those we have lost, and rally to support lifesaving research.”

Funds raised by Kicks for Cancer support ovarian cancer early detection and prevention research led by Dipanjan Chowdhury, PhD, the Svanberg Family Chair at Dana-Farber, largely due to the advocacy of beloved community member Jenna Swaim, who passed away in 2018. Because there are currently no established screening or detection methods for ovarian cancer, it is often discovered in later stages when treatment options are more limited. Chowdhury is leading efforts to advance a promising blood test for ovarian cancer that examines microRNAs, tiny molecules in the blood that may serve as early biomarkers for the disease—helping to predict if women at high genetic risk of ovarian cancer are likely to develop the disease.

“The ability to detect ovarian cancer early will greatly enhance our ability to treat patients effectively and provide them with hope for long-term survival,” said Chowdhury. “Kicks for Cancer is fueling research that has the potential to save countless lives, demonstrating the power of community to drive meaningful progress in cancer research.”

In September, 32 soccer teams took the field for Kicks for Cancer’s 19th season, proudly wearing the event’s signature pink and teal jerseys adorned with the names of loved ones.

“Our dream is to help people detect their cancer early, because if it can be caught sooner, women like Lois and Jenna might still be here,” said Trish. “This event is so important to us, and this research will help prevent us from losing another member of our community too soon.”

title: A legacy of care: Elevating palliative nursing education
body:
Winter 2025
By Kayla Carcone

When Shannon Robins reflects on her mother’s legacy, she sees a lifelong commitment to nursing, education, and compassionate care. Jean Cunningham, a nurse for over 40 years, worked her way from a staff nurse to an executive role in nursing, all while earning advanced degrees and raising her family. Even as she fought breast cancer for over a decade, Jean’s dedication to her profession and her patients never wavered.

“My mother was a lifelong nurse who worked tirelessly to educate and empower others,” Shannon shared. “Supporting this program is my way of carrying on what she started.” Shannon and her husband, Jason Robins, co-founder and CEO of DraftKings, a Jimmy Fund corporate sponsor, made a visionary $1 million gift to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, helping to launch a first-of-its-kind palliative care education program designed by nurses, for nurses. The first cohort begins this fall. The initiative aims to train 100% of Dana-Farber’s nursing staff in palliative care, ensuring that every patient—regardless of their stage of cancer—has access to supportive care that addresses their physical, emotional, and spiritual needs.

“Palliative care isn’t just about the end of someone’s life—it’s about improving quality of living at every stage of the journey.”

Shannon Robins

Palliative care is specialized medical care focused on relieving the symptoms, side effects, and stress of serious illness—helping patients maintain the best possible quality of life throughout treatment. “Palliative care isn’t just about the end of someone’s life—it’s about improving quality of living at every stage of the journey,” Shannon explained.

Vanessa Battista, Senior Nursing Director of Palliative Care, emphasized the program’s transformative potential. “This initiative is about empowering nurses to provide compassionate, patient-centered care during some of the most complex moments in oncology,” she said. “It’s a cultural shift that aligns with Dana-Farber’s commitment to total patient care.”

The program also reflects a broader movement to elevate the role of nurses in oncology. Nurses are often the first point of contact for patients and families, fielding difficult questions and providing critical support. Shannon hopes the program will give nurses the confidence and tools they need to navigate these moments with ease.

With Dana-Farber’s new dedicated inpatient cancer hospital and the future clinical collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, a Harvard-affiliated academic medical center, and its physician group, Harvard Medical Faculty Physicians, the program’s impact is poised to grow. Hundreds of new nurses will join Dana-Farber in the coming years, and Shannon envisions this training becoming a model for other healthcare organizations.

“My hope is that palliative care becomes a standard part of every patient’s experience,” Shannon said. “This gift is about honoring my mother’s legacy, but it’s also to ensure that every family feels supported during their experience.”

title: Trustee Science Committee fosters the next generation of researchers
body:
Winter 2025
By Cyrena Musset
Photography by Michael Blanchard

Shelby Roseman, PhD, and Amanda Smythers, PhD, were recently named the latest group of Trustee Science Committee Postdoctoral Fellows at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. The fellowship was launched in 2020 with donations from the Trustee Science Committee (TSC), a group of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute board members responsible for advancing research and cultivating scientific talent at all levels at Dana-Farber. Since the program’s inception, the TSC has raised more than $1 million to foster the next generation of cancer researchers.

Roseman is working to establish a collaborative research group to explore how epigenetic mechanisms drive cancer progression and drug resistance. Her work investigates the role of dysregulated repetitive DNA sequences, often dismissed as “junk DNA,” in shaping cancer cell states. By deepening our understanding of gene regulation in cancer, she aims to contribute to the development of innovative therapies. Roseman is currently conducting her research in the lab of Bradley Bernstein, MD, PhD, the Richard and Nancy Lubin Family Chair at Dana-Farber, a leader in epigenomics. Under Bernstein’s mentorship, she is building the foundation for her long-term goal of becoming a professor and advancing research on epigenetic regulation in cancer.

Smythers is driven by a deep passion for the scientific process and aspires to lead her own research group as a principal investigator (PI). Her scientific journey began with foundational research on topics ranging from photosynthetic electron transfer to tardigrade biology. As a postdoctoral fellow, she is integrating her background in fundamental science with translational research to address questions that can improve patient outcomes. Smythers is co-advised by Steve Gygi, PhD, at Harvard Medical School, and Bruce Spiegelman, PhD, who is the Stanley J. Korsmeyer, MD, Professor of Cell Biology and Medicine at Harvard Medical School, and Edward Chouchani, PhD, at Dana-Farber. Her primary work in the Spiegelman Lab focuses on applying her expertise in analytical chemistry to critical biological questions, while her involvement in the Gygi Lab allows her to advance mass spectrometry techniques. In the Chouchani Lab, she combines method development with biological implementation. This multidisciplinary training positions her to mentor the next generation of scientists while pursuing impactful research as a future PI.

“The Trustee Science Committee Fellowship plays a critical role in empowering individuals to pursue their passions and contribute to the future of science.”

Levi Garraway, MD, PhD, Dana-Farber Trustee

“Scientists come from all backgrounds, and their diverse perspectives drive innovation and discovery,” said Dana-Farber Trustee Levi Garraway, MD, PhD. “Supporting early career researchers is essential to ensure talent isn’t lost due to lack of resources. I give to the Trustee Science Committee Fellowship because it plays a critical role in empowering these individuals to pursue their passions and contribute to the future of science.”

title: A record-breaking year for Dana-Farber’s ASICS Falmouth Road Race team
body:
Winter 2025
By Sofi Elbadawi
Photography by Fidelis Teixeira

The ASICS Falmouth Road Race, a scenic seven-mile race along the Cape Cod coast, is one of the most well-known summer running events in New England, with race bibs highly sought after by runners from all over the globe. Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund is the official Legacy Partner of the Numbers for Nonprofits Program, the charity arm of the Falmouth Road Race. This year, on August 17, runners from Dana-Farber’s 2025 Falmouth Road Race team raised a record-breaking $1,105,554.90, the highest fundraising total in the team’s 23-year history, which exceeds $12.5 million to date for innovative research and compassionate patient care. The 2025 team also set a recruitment record, with 366 runners forming Dana-Farber’s largest Falmouth team yet. For many of these runners, the race was more than just a reason to lace up their sneakers—it was personal.

“I was diagnosed with invasive breast cancer in October 2023,” shared Catie Smith, a member of this year’s team. “Over the past 18 months, I’ve experienced firsthand how important the research and care options at Dana-Farber are, especially for patients like me,” she reflected.

Catie first ran the Falmouth Road Race 20 years ago. When the opportunity arose to run the seven-mile race again, this time in support of Dana-Farber, she didn’t hesitate.

“It was a no-brainer,” she said. “Everyone deserves access to high quality, research-based care. I hope that by running, I am doing my small part to advance the options available to future cancer patients.”

For others, like Trey Witter, the race was a way to honor loved ones who have benefited from Dana-Farber’s care. Trey ran this year’s Falmouth Road Race in honor of his father, who was diagnosed with leukemia.

“My dad would not be here if it wasn’t for the treatment he received at Dana-Farber.” Trey shared. “I’m honored to pay it forward to the doctors, nurses, and patients like my dad by running for Dana-Farber’s team.”

2025 also marked an incredible 20th consecutive Falmouth Road Race for Team Lanzoni/Bergeron founder Jim Kiley. Back in 2006, Jim was motivated to run with Dana-Farber after his friend David passed away from cancer. What started as a team of one has become a 20-year legacy, with hundreds of team members joining and thousands of dollars raised to support Dana-Farber’s lifesaving mission. When asked what keeps him coming back to the race year after year, Jim didn’t hesitate to share: “I do it for the doctors and patients at Dana-Farber. It’s that simple.”

title: Dana-Farber researchers awarded American Society of Hematology funding
body:
Winter 2025 
By Elyse Pleickhardt 

The American Society of Hematology (ASH) funds groundbreaking research on blood and bone marrow disorders. Over the past year, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers have earned a total of $845,000 in competitive ASH grants. 

Each Junior Faculty Scholar Award winner was granted $150,000. Recipient Roger Belizaire, MD, PhD, will continue to bridge gaps in the understanding of VEXAS syndrome, an inflammatory disorder that causes blood cell abnormalities. Zuzana Tothova, MD, PhD, aims to advance our understanding of blood cancer development in patients with inherited mutations in the gene RUNX1. Reid Merryman, MD, will continue to research immunotherapies for follicular lymphoma as alternatives to current, more toxic treatments. Additional ASH awards were granted to:  

  • Erin Parry, MD, PhD – 2024 Basic/Translational Fellow to Faculty Scholar Award: $125,000 
  • Nicoletta Cieri, MD, PhD – 2024 Basic/Translational Research Fellow Scholar Award: $100,000
  • Frederick Tsai, MD, PhD – 2024 Research Training Award for Fellows: $70,000
  • Miriam Osei, MD, MPH – 2025 Hematology Inclusion Pathway Fellow Award: $100,000 

“ASH is proud to recognize the work of Dana-Farber grantees and their innovative efforts to improve the lives of present and future blood cancer patients around the world,” said Belinda Avalos, MD, ASH president. We look forward to seeing the lifesaving impact of Dana-Farber ASH grantees’ dedicated research in the coming years.

title: Stephen B. Farber & Deirdre E. Curley make $1 million gift to honor family legacy
body:
Winter 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

Longtime Dana-Farber Cancer Institute supporters Trustee Stephen B. Farber and his wife Deirdre E. Curley made a $1 million gift to the Ellen Farber Schmidt Fund, which provides unrestricted support to Dana-Farber. The gift honors the memory of Steve’s sister, Ellen, who passed away in 2024, and continues the family’s legacy at Dana-Farber. Steve and Dee established the fund in 2024 with an initial gift of $250,000.

Steve is the son of Dr. Sidney Farber, who founded the Children’s Cancer Research Foundation (now Dana-Farber) in 1947 and is widely regarded as the father of modern chemotherapy. Steve joined the Board of Trustees in 1973 and is currently its longest-serving member. For 52 years, Steve and Dee have strongly supported presidential initiatives, capital campaigns, endowed chairs, and other Dana-Farber priorities.

Their professional lives have focused on public service. After completing studies at Harvard and Princeton, Steve worked to improve U.S. fiscal and intergovernmental policies and operations, starting with the new anti-poverty programs of the 1960s. He was an adviser to Indiana Congressman John Brademas, New Jersey Governor Richard J. Hughes, and Harvard University President Derek Bok. He then served as executive director of the National Governors’ Association; chairman of Concordia Group, a national advisory service on fiscal and intergovernmental affairs; and chief adviser for the County Council of Montgomery County, Maryland. Dee, a Wellesley College graduate, worked for the U.S. Bureau of Consumer Protection, the Massachusetts Council on Crime and Correction, and Wisconsin Governor Patrick J. Lucey as the state’s director of intergovernmental relations. She then served as the chief analyst for fiscal and trade issues at the National Governors’ Association, where she and Steve met, and as Assistant Director of the U.S. Trade and Development Agency.

“My father lives on at Dana-Farber, just as he does in us,” Steve said. “This conviction is what animates the gifts Dee and I have made over the years. We are proud to support many vitally important organizations. Dana-Farber is and always will be foremost among them.”

“While some of our past gifts have been for specific purposes, we understand the value and importance of unrestricted gifts. The overriding goal is to maximize support of all kinds in order to build on Dana-Farber’s extraordinary achievements over more than three quarters of a century.”

Steve Farber and Dee Curley

Steve and Dee added: “While some of our past gifts have been for specific purposes, we understand the value and importance of unrestricted gifts. The overriding goal is to maximize support of all kinds in order to build on Dana-Farber’s extraordinary achievements over more than three quarters of a century.”

title: A Deserving Salute
body:
Winter 2025
Photography by David Shopper

After more than a decade at the helm of Philanthropy Communications at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Assistant Vice President, Joyce Gallagher is embarking on her retirement journey.

Joyce joined the Division of Philanthropy at Dana-Farber in 2014, with over 35 years of communications and development experience—and a heart for the Dana-Farber mission. During her time here, she has led the Impact team, as well as the media relations and creative content teams. Joyce has seen us through more than 50 issues of Impact and its redesign, the Dana-Farber Campaign, the I Am Jimmy campaign, and countless Dana-Farber and Jimmy Fund features in the media. As a result, Dana-Farber has won numerous awards, including a 2025 AAMC Gold Award in Publications for Impact, and an international 2025 Gold Telly for a stellar Dana-Farber Campaign Close Video. In retirement, Joyce plans to consult and spend more time with her family. We salute Joyce for making a lasting impact and wish her an enjoyable and fulfilling next chapter!

Legendary rock icon Sir Roger Daltrey, lead singer of The Who and co-founder of Teen Cancer America (TCA), visited Dana-Farber Cancer Institute on Aug. 26 to mark the 10th anniversary of Dana-Farber’s partnership with TCA. title: The Dana-Farber Society
body:
Winter 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

The Dana-Farber Society (DFS) is a group of visionary donors who are changing lives and creating a legacy through a planned gift such as a bequest, life income gift, or beneficiary designation to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, the Jimmy Fund, the Friends of Dana-Farber, or the Pan-Mass Challenge. DFS members provide a dependable future source of funding to fuel Dana-Farber’s pursuit of innovative treatments and bring hope to patients and their families. Planned gifts support the revolutionary research, extraordinary care, and groundbreaking physician-scientists transforming the way the world thinks about cancer.

Priorities fueled by members’ gifts: 

  • cancer prevention and early detection 
  • next-generation cancer drugs 
  • signature total patient care 
  • cancer care equity 
  • pediatric and young adult treatment 

Visit Dana-Farber.org/DFS or contact Planned_Giving@dfci.harvard.edu to learn more.

body:

By Hannah White Hannah

Expect Miracles Foundation (EMF) received the 2025 Boston Red Sox Jimmy Fund Award—the Jimmy Fund’s highest honor—during a special on-field ceremony at Fenway Park. The presentation was a featured part of the annual WEEI/NESN Jimmy Fund Radio-Telethon presented by Arbella Insurance. Through events like the East Coast Golf Classic, galas, and marathon teams, EMF rallies the financial services industry, and beyond, to fuel breakthroughs and provide hope for patients and families facing cancer.

title: 2025 To-Do List
body:
Winter 2025 
Photography by John Deputy 

Before December 31: 

MAKE A GIFT THAT’S MATCHED 

Take advantage of our year-end matching challenge to support cancer research and care. When you donate to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund today, your gift doubles, thanks to a matching challenge from Arbella Insurance Group. And if your New Year’s resolution is to start a monthly gift, all your 2026 recurring gifts will be matched, up to $10,000! 

STOCK AND SECURITIES 

If you make a gift of appreciated securities before the end of the calendar year, you may be entitled to a charitable deduction on this year’s federal income taxes and may also avoid capital gains tax on the appreciation of the asset. These tax savings could increase the value of your gift to Dana-Farber and the Jimmy Fund at a decreased cost to you. Through a partnership with The Boston Foundation, you can also donate privately held C-Corp stock for the benefit of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. 

INDIVIDUAL RETIREMENT ACCOUNT (IRA) 

If you are 70½ or older, you can give up to $108,000 to Dana-Farber directly from your IRA without paying income taxes on the transfer. Plus, if you are 73 or older, your gift may satisfy your required minimum distribution and lower your taxable income. No matter your age, you can designate Dana-Farber and the Jimmy Fund as the beneficiary of all or a percentage of your IRA and it will pass to us tax-free after your lifetime. 

DONOR-ADVISED FUND (DAF) 

Now is a great time to distribute a donation to Dana-Farber and the Jimmy Fund from your DAF. Recommend a grant from your DAF by December 31 to fuel groundbreaking discoveries and initiatives into the new year. You can name Dana-Farber as a beneficiary of your donor-advised fund as well! 

REVIEW AND UPDATE ACCOUNT BENEFICIARIES 

The end of the year is a great time to review beneficiary designations on your bank, investment, and retirement accounts. Of course, loved ones are the first people to consider. After that, providing for causes you care about like Dana-Farber is an excellent way to demonstrate your values and make an impact on future generations. 

To learn more, visit jimmyfund.org/get-involved/give.

title: A Message from Melany Duval
body:
Winter 2025

Dear Friends,

As I reflect on this past year, I am filled with immense gratitude for the generosity and unwavering commitment of our Dana-Farber community. Your steadfast support has been a driving force behind so many of our achievements, and it is because of you that we have been able to navigate challenges and embrace new opportunities with hope and determination.

This year brought unexpected uncertainties due to changes in federal policy. However, your belief in our mission never wavered. Your dedication has enabled us to continue our vital work and celebrate remarkable milestones, including the installment of eight leaders into endowed chair and professorship positions. These endowed positions, made possible by your philanthropy, provide permanent funding that will sustain groundbreaking scientific and clinical advancements for generations to come. Together, we are opening doors to extraordinary possibilities, and we are premiering a new section in this issue that highlights some of this work.

We are especially grateful for unrestricted gifts that empower us to innovate and expand our efforts in research and treatment. The largest donor for unrestricted gifts is the Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), which we are proud to feature on our cover. Since its founding in 1980, the PMC has contributed well over $1 billion to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, a tremendous feat that continues to grow. This year alone the PMC raised a record-breaking $78 million with 100% of rider-raised funds going to Dana-Farber. The compassion and determination of PMC riders inspire us all, and their commitment to defying cancer is a powerful reminder of what we can accomplish together.

Thanks to your support, we have built a strong foundation for advancing cancer research, treatment, and care for every patient who walks through our doors. As we look ahead, I am filled with hope for all that we will accomplish. I look forward to celebrating each new advance with you, knowing none of these achievements would be possible without your partnership.

With heartfelt appreciation,

Melany N. Duval
Senior Vice President and Chief Philanthropy Officer
Seven-year Pan-Mass Challenge rider

title: Defying Cancer 26.2 miles at a time
photo_credit: Photography by Justin Knight, Kelly Dillon Photography
body:
Fall 2025
By Sofi Elbadawi
Photography by Justin Knight, Kelly Dillon Photography

On Monday, April 21, more than 500 runners completed the 129th Boston Marathon® as part of the 2025 Dana-Farber Marathon Challenge (DFMC) team. This year’s DFMC athletes collectively raised over $8.3 million and counting for the Claudia Adams Barr Program in Innovative Basic Cancer Research, which provides funding for groundbreaking ideas at their earliest stages, propelling them toward discovery and potential cures.

Among this year’s DFMC team members was Tara Kenney, a Boston native whose connection to the team was deeply personal. Running the Boston Marathon had always been a lifelong dream for Tara, but it never felt like an achievable goal. That all changed when her father was diagnosed with glioblastoma multiforme grade IV (GBM) in February 2024. “Seeing my father face his diagnosis with grace, strength, and humor inspired me to do something bigger than myself and to join the DFMC team in his honor,” she shared. Motivated by her father’s courage, Tara was able to accomplish her goal of completing the Boston Marathon, crossing the finish line in Copley Square with a photo of her father raised high.

For Tara, running the Boston Marathon with the DFMC team was not only a personal achievement, but also a testament to the power of community and shared purpose. “I feel so lucky to have met teammates who supported me through my marathon training, but also through the loss of my father,” she shared. “Over the course of the season, there is a bond that forms amongst teammates that can’t be described, and I feel so lucky to have been a part of it.”

Tara’s commitment to Dana-Farber’s mission is fueled by her father’s legacy. “Glioblastoma multiforme grade IV still does not have a cure,” she noted. “I want to continue supporting Dana-Farber Cancer Institute so that future patients and families facing this disease have options.”

Since its first steps in 1990, the DFMC team has directed 100% of funds raised—more than $140 million to date—to the Claudia Adams Barr Program in Innovative Basic Cancer Research. Anthony G. Letai, MD, PhD, a Claudia Adams Barr Program Investigator, emphasized the importance of basic science research. “The Claudia Adams Barr Program in Innovative Basic Cancer Research provides funds for new ideas going in new directions,” he explained. “It can be challenging to secure funding for new research directions through more traditional pathways. With so much uncertainty surrounding National Institutes of Health funding, the role of this program has never been more important.”

“Seeing my father face his diagnosis with grace, strength, and humor inspired me to do something bigger than myself.”

Tara Kenney, 2025 DFMC Runner

Support from the DFMC team has enabled researchers like Letai to explore innovative approaches that can lead to significant advancements in cancer treatment. “For me, it gave me the ability to go in a new direction at several points in my career,” he shared. “In one case, the eventual impact was a new treatment for both acute myeloid leukemia and chronic lymphocytic
leukemia.”

Thanks to runners like Tara and researchers like Letai, the DFMC team is making strides in the fight against cancer, 26.2 miles at a time.

title: Impactful Progress: President and CEO Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD, reflects on his first year and strategic vision for the future of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
body:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

As Dana-Farber Cancer Institute marks a transformative year under the leadership of President and CEO and Susan Smith Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD, Impact spoke with him about the significant milestones achieved and the exciting path ahead.

Ebert stepped into his new leadership role at a pivotal moment for Dana-Farber, with plans for a new inpatient cancer hospital, major ambulatory expansion, and a rising demand for cancer care while the Institute simultaneously faced changes in federal research funding. Reflecting on his first year, Ebert shared insights into leading during a time of uncertainty. “It’s been an incredible privilege,” he remarked. “I’m proud of our agility in responding to changes in our external environment while maintaining our culture and our sense of mission.”

Soon after assuming his role, Ebert initiated an Institute-wide strategic planning process. Illustrating a commitment to maintaining culture throughout the organization, the strategic planning process engaged faculty and staff across Dana-Farber for their input to develop the plan for the future of the Institute. Ebert focused on the “big three” pillars—research, clinical, and education—as foundational to Dana-Farber’s future, specifically reaffirming Dana-Farber’s equal commitment to cancer research and clinical care while increasing the emphasis on education at all levels.

“I’m proud of our agility in responding to changes in our external environment while maintaining our culture and our sense of mission.”

Benjamin L. Ebert

Looking to the future, Ebert is focused on how to provide the best possible environment for basic, translational, and clinical research. He noted that artificial intelligence is poised to reshape oncology research, driving advancements from basic science to clinical trials. Ebert emphasized the potential of AI in transforming Dana-Farber’s future: “Our investment into artificial intelligence will influence diverse types of research and the future of clinical oncology.”

Clinically, a central component of Ebert’s strategic growth plan is the development of a new state-of-the-art cancer hospital in collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. This facility will integrate inpatient and ambulatory care, enhancing patient experiences and improving outcomes. Additionally, improving care for our pediatric oncology patients includes a proposed proton therapy facility and further developing our collaboration with Boston Children’s Hospital.

Recognizing the importance of knowledge in driving innovation, Ebert also stressed that Dana-Farber is committed to expanding its educational initiatives. “A major part of the strategic plan is expanding our education efforts,” he explained. This initiative aims to enhance educational materials for our patients and opportunities to train future oncology healthcare professionals, positioning Dana-Farber as a leading source of cancer knowledge.

Ebert emphasized that philanthropy plays a crucial role in each of Dana-Farber’s initiatives, providing us with ongoing support for our greatest priorities. “Philanthropy enables us to accomplish ambitious research objectives and deliver compassionate care. Our donor community is vital for transforming our institution,” said Ebert. Now more than ever, the support of donors is essential for realizing the vision of the new cancer hospital and advancing groundbreaking research.

Ebert is clear that accessible cancer care remains at the heart of Dana-Farber’s mission: From building a network of clinics across Massachusetts and New England, to mammogram vans that offer screenings in communities that otherwise may not have immediate access to Dana-Farber-level care. “We are expanding our network of clinics and working with community partners to improve coordination of care,” said Ebert.

As Ebert looks ahead to his second year, he is excited about defining cancer care for years to come with the Future Cancer Hospital, advancing research, and expanding educational efforts. “The opportunities ahead are greater than ever, and it’s incredibly motivating to be part of this transformative journey.”

title: Conquering blood cancers is focus of Blood Cancer United grants
body:
Fall 2025
By Kathy Clute
Photography by Sam Ogden

Each year, nearly 200,000 Americans are diagnosed with leukemia, lymphoma, myeloma, or another bloodborne cancer. Blood Cancer United has awarded $4.2 million in grants to eight Dana-Farber physician-scientists working to better understand, treat, and potentially cure these often deadly diseases.

Andrew Lane, MD, PhD, and Anthony Letai, MD, PhD, received the organization’s prestigious multiyear Discovery Grants, which support groundbreaking research of blood cancers’ properties and vulnerabilities to advance treatments for them.

Lane, associate chief of the Division of Hematologic Neoplasia, is exploring how existing drugs that block the PI3 kinase gamma pathway in solid tumors could benefit certain patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

Letai’s work focuses on improving the performance of CAR T cells—natural immune cells that are genetically modified to recognize and attack the proteins on the surface of cancer cells—against blood cancers. While CAR T cells have produced lifesaving results in some cases, their effectiveness is limited by how long they survive in the body.

Blood Cancer United, in collaboration with the Follicular Lymphoma Foundation and the Institute for Follicular Lymphoma Innovation, also awarded grants to Philippe Armand, MD, PhD, and Mark Murakami, MD. Armand is the chief of the Lymphoma Division and the Harold and Virginia Lash Endowed Chair in Lymphoma Research at Dana-Farber.

Follicular lymphoma (FL) is an often incurable type of indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma. It is typically managed through a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy that can have detrimental side effects and negatively impact quality of life.

Armand and co-principal investigator Reid Merryman, MD, are conducting a phase two clinical trial of a chemotherapy-free regimen based on bispecific antibodies in patients with previously untreated FL. If successful, the trial could pave the way for a new, effective, and chemotherapy-free frontline treatment option for FL patients. Murakami is focused on understanding how some lymphoma cells survive this treatment and go on to cause relapse, with the goal of selecting patients for this type of therapy and ultimately devising improved future treatments.

Other Blood Cancer United grantees are Rizwan Romee, MD (Clinical Trials), Reina Takeda, MD, PhD, and Nicoletta Cieri, MD, PhD (Special Fellows), and Rachel Mersfelder, a medical student studying with the David G. Nathan, MD, Professor of Pediatrics at Harvard Medical School Kimberly Stegmaier, MD [Student Mentorship and Research Training (SMART)].

“Research is the key to unlocking the complexities of blood cancers, and we look forward with great anticipation to the results of these Dana-Farber studies and their positive impact on quality of life for blood cancer patients and their families,” said E. Anders Kolb, MD, Blood Cancer United’s president and CEO.

title: Dana-Farber faculty are part of “grand challenge” to defeat childhood tumors
body:
Fall 2025
By Kathy Clute
Photography by Sam Ogden

Dana-Farber has been awarded more than $3 million in funding as part of a Cancer Grand Challenge to find new treatments for solid tumors in children. “Outcomes for some pediatric cancers have not improved in more than 30 years,” said David Scott, PhD, director of Cancer Grand Challenges.

“Standard treatment regimens continue to rely on cytotoxic agents and, often, radiotherapy, which induce an alarming rate of severe health effects later in life.”

In 2025, about 15,000 U.S. children and adolescents ages birth to 19 are expected to be diagnosed with cancer, according to the American Cancer Society. Solid tumors, which include brain tumors, neuroblastoma, and others, make up a significant portion of these cases.

The Dana-Farber faculty members working on the Grand Challenge are part of a collaborative, international team called PROTECT—Harnessing PROTEin Degradation for Advanced Childhood Tumors. Protein degraders are an emerging class of therapeutic agents designed to target and eliminate specific proteins within cancer cells. Kimberly Stegmaier, MD, is leading the Dana-Farber contingent, which includes Scott Armstrong, MD, PhD, the Ted Williams Chair at Dana-Farber; Cigall Kadoch, PhD, the Meredith and Billy Starr Investigator at Dana-Farber; Eric Fischer, PhD, the Joseph Deitch Family Chair at Dana-Farber; and Dana-Farber President and CEO Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD, the Richard and Susan Smith Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School. Stegmair is the David G. Nathan, MD, Professor of Pediatrics at Harvard Medical School as well as chair of the Pediatric Oncology Department. Team PROTECT is led by Stefan Pfister, MD, from the German Cancer Research Center/DKFZ in Germany, uniting clinicians, advocates, and scientists across 10 institutions and five countries.

“Cures will require innovative interventions that specifically target the unique biology of pediatric tumors,” Stegmaier said. “Our goal is to develop a new generation of therapeutic approaches for children with Ewing sarcoma, neuroblastoma, synovial sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, ependymoma, and high-grade glioma by targeting proteins previously thought to be undruggable.”

The team is developing small molecule prototype drugs that work by bringing together proteins expressed in the cancer cells and a special enzyme called an E3 ligase. This enzyme targets the protein for destruction, allowing the cell to dispose of it.

The goal is to advance the most promising project to the point where an Investigational New Drug (IND) application can be filed with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, demonstrating that a drug is reasonably safe for initial testing in humans. If the IND application is approved, Phase 1 clinical trials can begin.

Cancer Grand Challenges is a global research initiative that identifies the toughest challenges in cancer research. Team PROTECT is funded by Cancer Research UK, the National Cancer Institute, The Spanish Association Against Cancer, and KiKa (Children Cancer Free Foundation).

title: Smith Family support inspires others to help speed multiple myeloma research
body:
Fall 2025
By Brittany Flaherty
Photography by Sam Ogden

Dana-Farber is a global leader in developing new treatments to help patients with multiple myeloma (MM), having played a critical role in developing and testing nearly all of the 19 new lifesaving MM therapies approved since 2003. Thanks to these advances, MM patients now live three- to five-times longer than they did two decades ago. Unfortunately, some MM disease subtypes do not respond to existing treatments, and many patients who respond initially develop resistance to these drugs over time. Because of this, MM continues to exact a heavy toll, claiming the lives of more than 100,000 people worldwide each year.

At Dana-Farber, Paul Richardson, MD, director of clinical research at the Jerome Lipper Multiple Myeloma Center, is poised to address the urgent needs of these patients. Richardson and his team are internationally renowned for spearheading clinical trials that elevate the standard of MM care, bringing new hope to patients with difficult forms of the disease. Philanthropy is critical to their efforts, and Richardson has found an important partner in Robert and Dana Smith, who recently made a $3 million gift to continue supporting his advanced clinical trials research. This gift builds on the Smiths’ past support of Richardson’s clinical trials work, which inspired a remarkable four-fold increase in donor commitments to MM clinical research from other supporters. This collective philanthropy helped Richardson expand his team by 46% in 4 years, which in turn led to an 18.5% increase in active MM trials from 2020 to 2024.

“This advanced clinical trials program is the tip of the spear in addressing the most vexing challenges in multiple myeloma.”

Robert Smith

“Our team is determined to develop and refine new therapies and treatment strategies for patients with the most challenging forms of multiple myeloma to further improve outcomes,” said Richardson. “We are profoundly grateful that Rob and Dana have partnered with us toward this goal, and for the entire community that they inspire to support our crucial efforts to help patients and our overall mission to turn the tide on myeloma.”

Expanded clinical trials have helped expedite the delivery of new MM drugs to patients at an unprecedented pace, as evidenced by FDA approval for eight new MM therapies since 2020. Continued support will help Richardson sustain and expand this robust portfolio of clinical trials, expediting his team’s ability to find the next breakthrough treatments.

“This advanced clinical trials program is the tip of the spear in addressing the most vexing challenges in multiple myeloma,” said Robert.

“Translating basic discoveries into more therapeutic options that can improve patient quality of life is precisely where targeted philanthropy can unlock the future of living with, and ultimately curing, this disease. Paul and his impressive team have the breadth of talent, creativity, and the unstoppable will to build on their impressive body of work. These are dollars well spent!”

title: Advancing early detection research through the Larry and Susan Marx Fund
body:
Fall 2025
By Casey Repasy

For decades, Larry and Susan Marx have been steadfast supporters of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. Larry served as a Trustee from 1994 to 2005, and both he and Susan, members of the Dana-Farber Society, have contributed more than $5 million providing transformational support to population sciences research—a field that explores how social, environmental, behavioral, and genetic factors influence cancer risk and outcomes. Most recently, they established the Larry and Susan Marx Fund for Early Detection with a $2.6 million gift, supporting efforts to detect and screen cancers earlier and improve treatment outcomes.

According to the World Health Organization, about 20 million new cancer cases are diagnosed worldwide each year. Nearly half go undetected until the disease has progressed and spread, making treatment more difficult. Impactful gifts like the Marxs’ are critical to changing this reality.

Their funding supports the work of Catherine Marinac, PhD, and her team. That team is developing cutting-edge early detection methods to identify cancer at its earliest, most treatable stages. One such method is the GRAIL Galleri multicancer early detection (MCED) blood test, which can detect 50 different types of cancer with a simple blood draw—many of which have no effective screening options.

“We believe MCED tests hold immense promise as a minimally invasive, convenient way to detect cancer signals before symptoms appear and increase the number of cancers that can be detected through screening,” Marinac said. “With support from Larry and Susan, we are able to pursue new cancer screening trials that could fundamentally change how we screen.”

“Susan and I remain deeply impressed by the dedication of the outstanding researchers at Dana-Farber, and we are honored to support this important work.”

Larry Marx

While the MCED test shows promise, more work remains. A patient with a positive GRAIL test currently has about a 55% chance of a false positive and a 45% chance of having cancer. Further research is needed to determine how to use these tests in clinical settings.

Both Marinac and Elizabeth O’Donnell, MD, director of Early Detection and Prevention of Malignant Conditions within Dana-Farber’s Centers for Early Detection and Interception, believes patients with elevated cancer risk—due to inherited genetic mutations or family history—may be optimal candidates for the MCED test. The INFORM study is also establishing a gold standard for implementing an MCED test with rapid, coordinated follow-up to improve care delivery. The study also evaluates strategies to minimize the anxiety that patients face when undergoing cancer screening.

Thanks to the Larry and Susan Marx Fund for Early Detection, the research team will screen 1,000 new individuals with elevated cancer risk to answer these critical questions.

“Susan and I remain deeply impressed by the dedication of the outstanding researchers at Dana-Farber, and we are honored to support this important work,” Larry said.

title: A home run for hope: A Father’s tribute advances pediatric research
body:
Fall 2025
By Amber Sinicrope

The late Robert P. Cingolani, DPM—affectionately known as “Doc”—was a dedicated physician, devoted father, and cherished community member. He made a transformative $2 million estate gift to support pediatric cancer research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in memory of his son, Michael, who passed away from bone cancer at the age of 19.

Michael was treated at Dana-Farber as a teenager after being diagnosed with sarcoma in high school. Exceptionally kind and courageous, Michael became a source of strength and guidance for others in his peer group, offering advice and support to fellow patients navigating their own cancer journeys.

“Not a day went by that Doc didn’t mention Michael,” said close family friend Katie McGowan. “They had a profound bond and Doc was so appreciative of the care Michael received at Dana-Farber and he was determined to do something meaningful in his memory.” This extraordinary contribution will accelerate groundbreaking research and enhance treatment options for children and adolescents facing cancer, ensuring that Michael’s legacy will inspire hope and healing for generations to come.

Often described as authentic, quirky, and tenacious, Doc passed away in March 2022 at the age of 97. His long and remarkable life was marked by service, compassion, and an irrepressible spirit that left an indelible mark on all who met him. After serving as a medic throughout World War II, including during D-Day operations, he used the GI Bill to become a podiatrist—earning a reputation as a caring and trusted physician. Outside of his practice, Doc was a passionate Red Sox fan, an avid fly fisherman, and a beloved youth baseball umpire who spent decades supporting the local New Bedford Legion team. Doc’s generosity extended far beyond the clinic and the ballfield, as his unwavering support for friends and family was legendary, as was his unique personality.

“Doc was unapologetically himself. He was truly one of a kind and helping others fueled him,” said McGowan. “And once Doc was in your corner, he was there for good. He showed up for everything—weddings, performances, graduations, you name it.”

Doc’s commitment to cancer research was also shaped by the loss of his niece to breast cancer in her 40s, deepening his resolve to contribute to progress in cancer care. Doc’s estate gift will directly support innovative research led by Dana-Farber’s esteemed pediatric oncologists. Through this remarkable act of philanthropy, Doc ensures that both his and Michael’s legacies will endure. His story is a moving reminder that generosity, in all its forms, can make a lasting mark on the world.

title: Russ Agrusa honors late wife by fueling colorectal cancer research
body:
Fall 2025
By Caitlin Henault
Photography by David Fox Photographer

Basic research and discovery science often power the greatest breakthroughs in cancer research, paving the way for enhanced treatments, improved patient outcomes, and renewed hope for individuals with cancer and their families. For Russ Agrusa, this concept drives his visionary commitment to supporting innovative research initiatives at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

“Electricity was discovered 400 years before we had computer chips and iPhones,” said Russ. “Progress can seem slow when we’re dealing with what is very complex biology—we’re still in the discovery phase. That’s why cancer research is so important: you can’t treat something if you don’t understand how it works.”

Russ and his late wife, Paula, established the Project P Fund in 2014 with a goal of empowering researchers at Dana-Farber to develop more effective targeted and immune-based therapies for patients with colorectal cancer. Since Paula’s death in 2016, Russ has continued to honor her legacy through ongoing support for the Project P Fund. With a generous new gift of $2 million, Russ will provide critical funding for projects designed to transform immune-based therapies, enhance precision medicine, and advance prevention, early detection, and interception of the disease.

“Funding from the Project P Fund will help us deliver promising new immunotherapy approaches that will prolong and improve quality of life for patients, match patients with medicines that target the specific gene alterations driving their tumors, and leverage artificial intelligence to develop new early detection tests and interventions,” said Kimmie Ng, MD, MPH, associate chief of the Division of Gastrointestinal Oncology, director of the Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center, and co-director of the Colon and Rectal Cancer Center. Ng leads the Project P team alongside Jeffrey Meyerhardt, MD, MPH, chief clinical research officer, co-director of the Colon and Rectal Cancer Center, and the Douglas Gray Woodruff Chair in Colorectal Cancer Research at Dana-Farber; Marios Giannakis, MD, PhD; and Benjamin Schlechter, MD.

With Paula’s legacy top of mind, Russ believes that these efforts—combined with the power of emerging technologies like artificial intelligence—will bring the power of more personalized immune-based treatments to patients with colorectal cancer.

“My dream is a world where every patient with cancer can receive a personalized treatment that fires up their own immune system to fight their disease,” Russ said. “It may sound like science fiction, but every one of these scientific discoveries adds to the arsenal of knowledge that will bring us closer to that world.”

title: Transformational gift expands international fellowships in breast oncology
body:
Fall 2025
By Stephanie Lowitt
Photography by Capehart Photography

Over the past 13 years, the Goldfarb and Rudkin Family International Fellowships in Breast Oncology at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute have accelerated scientific breakthroughs, fostered career growth through mentorship and collaboration, and advanced cancer care for patients around the world.

This extraordinary program has funded 11 fellows hailing from six different countries—Spain, Brazil, Australia, Israel, Canada, and Italy. Now, thanks to an additional gift from William and Maureen Goldfarb, this premier training program will continue and expand.

This prestigious fellowship engages a multipronged approach to supporting expertise in breast oncology. The program broadens and strengthens the talent and knowledge available at Dana-Farber by attracting and retaining experts from around the world. Fellows obtain valuable firsthand research experience during their tenure, learn how to run clinical trials, set up research infrastructure, evaluate outcomes, and more. The fellows then have the opportunity to participate in academic publications by producing original reports, reviewing papers, and making presentations. As part of Dana-Farber’s equal commitment to patient care and research, the fellows gain expertise in the clinical treatment of patients by caring for breast cancer patients in the clinic with the supervision of faculty mentors.

Thanks to past program support from the Goldfarbs, three fellows have gone on to hold faculty positions at Dana-Farber and Harvard Medical School, and many other graduates now maintain leadership roles in medicine in their native countries. This brings Dana-Farber’s knowledge of cancer care and the remarkable progress the fellows make in cancer medicine to patients worldwide and provides Dana-Farber a valuable link to other institutions here and abroad working on transformational research.

Thanks in great part to the Goldfarb’s ongoing support, the Division of Breast Oncology at Dana-Farber is internationally known as a space that fosters innovation, collaboration, and the development of new models for understanding and treating breast cancer globally. As Goldfarb and Rudkin Family Fellow, Paolo Tarantino, MD, shared, “For many years, I dreamt of joining the breast team at Dana-Farber. No other place in the world, indeed, has had such a major impact in the way we treat and conceive of this disease, and no other place in the world would have been more appropriate for my scientific growth.”

Sara Tolaney, MD, MPH, co-director of the fellowship, understands the value of investing in early career oncologists. “The Goldfarb and Rudkin Family International Fellowships in Breast Oncology have been a cornerstone of innovation and excellence—training the next generation of leaders who are advancing care, accelerating research, and shaping the future of breast cancer treatment. Its graduates are not only making breakthroughs in research, but also bringing compassionate, cutting-edge care to patients around the world.”

title: Susan G. Komen strengthens commitment to breast cancer research
photo_credit: Photography by Justin Knight, Kayla Prasek
body:
Fall 2025
By Kayla McMahon
Photography by Justin Knight, Kayla Prasek

Susan G. Komen, a world-leading nonprofit breast cancer organization, remains committed to driving progress through innovation. In 2024, Komen reaffirmed its dedication to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute by awarding three new Career Transition Awards totaling $1.95 million, alongside 12 active research grants. This investment underscores Komen’s ongoing support for groundbreaking studies and improving outcomes for those affected by breast cancer.

The Career Transition Awards were granted to Kristen Brantley, PhD; Jun Nishida, PhD; and Nolan Priedigkeit, MD, PhD. These promising scientists are poised to make significant strides in breast cancer research. Brantley focuses on improving outcomes for young women, a group facing unique challenges and often overlooked in clinical trials. Her work aims to uncover biological factors that contribute to poorer survival rates, offering hope for more tailored treatments.

Nishida and Priedigkeit are committed to deepening our understanding of breast cancer. Their research explores the molecular intricacies of the disease, seeking to unravel the complexities that have long eluded scientists and identify innovative ways to exploit them therapeutically. Together, these three early career investigators represent the next generation of leaders in breast cancer research, supported by Komen’s visionary funding.

The 12 additional recipients of research grants at Dana-Farber include esteemed physician-scientists Myles Brown, MD; Sarah Hill, MD, PhD; Jose Pablo Leone, MD; Heather Parsons, MD, MPH; Jennifer Ligibel, MD; Nancy Lin, MD; Filipa Lynce, MD; Elizabeth Mittendorf, MD, PhD, MHCM; Ann Partridge, MD, MPH; Kornelia Polyak, MD, PhD; Sara Tolaney, MD, MPH; and Adrienne Waks, MD. Each investigator contributes to a tapestry of innovation, weaving together insights that have the potential to transform breast cancer treatment.

Paula Schneider, president and CEO of Susan G. Komen, emphasized the organization’s faith in Dana-Farber. “At Komen, we believe deeply in the power of science to save lives—and we have great confidence in Dana-Farber’s ability to lead the way,” said Schneider. “Our support of their groundbreaking research beautifully reflects our shared commitment to improving outcomes for all people facing breast cancer. By funding innovative investigations and rising scientific leaders, we’re one step closer to a world without breast cancer.”

With breast cancer incidence rates rising, particularly among younger women, the urgency for innovative science has never been greater. Susan G. Komen’s steadfast support for Dana-Farber is a powerful catalyst for finding solutions and improving lives. Together, they are forging a path toward a future where breast cancer is a challenge all patients can overcome.

title: V Foundation grants power colorectal cancer research
body:
Fall 2025
By Kayla McMahon

The V Foundation for Cancer Research once again demonstrated its remarkable generosity and commitment to advancing cancer research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute by awarding $1.4 million in grants to two exceptional investigators. Grant recipients Edward Chouchani, PhD, and Gabriel Griffin, MD, are leading projects that are pivotal in enhancing the understanding and treatment of colorectal cancers, the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States, because of the invaluable support of the V Foundation.

Chouchani’s research is supported by the V Foundation’s Adult Translational Grant, which focuses on moving novel strategies from the laboratory to human clinical trials. He investigates how cancer cells manipulate nutrient usage to grow and spread, particularly through enzymes called creatine kinases (CKs). These enzymes are crucial for the growth and sustenance of colon cancer cells but not for healthy ones, presenting a unique target for treatment. Chouchani developed a promising new medicine that inhibits CKs, effectively killing cancer cells reliant on these enzymes. His next step is to test this medicine in animal models, a critical precursor to human trials.

“We are grateful for their dedication to accelerating victory over cancer® and saving lives.”

Kara Coleman, PhD, V Foundation for Cancer Research

Griffin’s research is funded by the V Foundation’s V Scholar Grant, which supports early career, tenure-track faculty in their laboratory-based or translational research endeavors. He aims to enhance immunotherapy by understanding how cancer cells evade the immune system. Griffin’s lab investigates ancient viruses embedded in human DNA, typically silenced by epigenetic repressors. By activating these viruses in cancer cells, Griffin hopes to stimulate the immune system to target and destroy tumors, potentially paving the way for new cancer therapies, especially for patients unresponsive to existing immunotherapies.

Kara Coleman, PhD, Vice President of Grants and Research at the V Foundation, expressed her enthusiasm for the recipients. “We are proud to fund the best and brightest scientists in the cancer research space and are thrilled to congratulate Drs. Ed Chouchani and Gabe Griffin as V Foundation grantees,” she shared. “We are grateful for their dedication to accelerating Victory Over Cancer® and saving lives.”

The V Foundation’s generosity is crucial in helping Dana-Farber sustain its momentum of research and discovery. Through their support, investigators like Chouchani and Griffin are translating groundbreaking research into new treatment options, which is improving outcomes and offering hope to cancer patients worldwide. By investing in pioneering scientists, the V Foundation is ensuring that innovative therapies reach patients’ bedsides and helping to create a future where all cancers are treatable.

title: Basic research is focus of Mathers Charitable Foundation grants
body:
Fall 2025
By Kathy Clute
Photography by Sam Ogden

The G. Harold and Leila Y. Mathers Charitable Foundation has awarded Dana-Farber $1.47 million to support two Institute researchers investigating how cancer develops and how cells detect and respond to viral infections.

“We believe that transformative breakthroughs in cancer will come from a thorough understanding of the fundamental mechanisms by which it arises and grows,” said Zach Handelman, vice president and treasurer of the Mathers Foundation. “We feel privileged to fund this work at Dana-Farber and look forward to the new knowledge it will generate.”

Since 1991, the foundation has invested more than $17 million in basic and translational research at the Institute. The 2024 grants were awarded to microbiologist Philip Kranzusch, PhD, and pediatric oncologist David Pellman, MD, Margaret M. Dyson Professorship in Pediatric Oncology at Harvard Medical School.

Kranzusch’s team is investigating how cells respond to viral pathogens and how those signaling pathways can be harnessed to create potential new therapies for cancer and autoimmune diseases. “Human cells have a set of protein sensors that detect viral infections and quickly trigger immune responses,” said Kranzusch. “Interestingly, key components of antiviral immunity evolved billions of years ago in bacteria as mechanisms to defend against viruses called phages.”

The lab aims to understand how two bacterial defense systems work together to prevent phages from reproducing, possibly by forming complex structures that degrade viral DNA. The research team has discovered human immune genes with structural similarities, which may enable them to identify previously unknown proteins that play a role in the human immune response to viral infections.

Pellman and his colleagues study cell division and chromosome segregation errors in cancer and the impact of these faults on cancer genome structure. Nuclear atypia—unusual changes in the size and shape of cell nuclei—are a common feature of many tumors and have been used since the 1920s to assess tumor severity and predict outcomes. Previous research funded by the Mathers Foundation has found that these nuclear changes significantly affect genome rearrangements in human cancers.

It is possible that DNA changes and shifts in gene expression in atypical nuclei might be influenced by the formation of nuclear bodies around chromosomes after cells divide. Pellman is using advanced single-cell genomic technologies developed in his lab to zero in on specific nuclear bodies known as MN/53BP1, which are part of the cell’s response to DNA damage. A better understanding of how cells respond to DNA damage could lead to improved cancer treatments.

title: Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation gift focuses on cancer interception
photo_credit: Photography by Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation
body:
Fall 2025
By Kathy Clute
Photography by Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation

Cancer of the pancreas is a leading cause of cancer death because it is usually not discovered until it has progressed to a late stage, when treatment options are limited. A $1.25 million gift to Dana-Farber from the Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation seeks to change that by supporting research focused on ways the disease might be detected—and intercepted—before it can be seen on CT scans or other imaging modalities.

Ilene Beal was a pioneering banking executive from Wellesley, Mass., who generously mentored other women in business for years before her death from cancer in 2015. She is remembered as a warm, caring person who was always thinking of others and ready to help. For nearly 10 years, Beal was treated by Jeffrey Wisch, MD, who was a senior physician at Dana-Farber.

The Beal Foundation’s 2025 gift of $1.25 million establishes the Ilene Beal Fund to Eradicate Cancer and builds on past gifts, including to the Ilene Beal & Jeffrey S. Wisch, MD, Clinical Investigator Fund.

The latest gift will support research led by Brian Wolpin, MD, MPH, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Center and the Robert T. and Judith B. Hale Chair in Pancreatic Cancer at Dana-Farber. Wolpin is testing the ability of small molecule inhibitors to target mutations in the KRAS oncogene found in precursor lesions called pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN). These lesions cannot be detected using current imaging techniques, and more than 90 percent of pancreatic cancers have KRAS gene mutations.

KRAS inhibitors have shown promise in patients with advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas, and Wolpin, who is also director, Hale Family Center for Pancreatic Cancer Research, intends to use those molecules to develop new imaging methods and interception strategies. This will permit oncologists to identify high-risk PanINs and treat them before they have a chance to become invasive cancers. For example, radiolabeled versions of the inhibitors could be used with PET imaging to find lesions that cannot now be detected, allowing them to be non-invasively monitored over time.

In 2025, 67,440 Americans are expected to be diagnosed with pancreatic cancer and an estimated 51,980 people may die from it, according to the National Cancer Institute.

“Ilene was a mentor, a role model, a collaborative and talented executive who worked hard at everything she did, because she believed that with dedication and focused work one could accomplish anything,” said Brian Potts, a trustee of the Ilene Beal Charitable Foundation. “She would be thrilled to fund this pathbreaking research because she knew firsthand the challenges of cancer.”

title: IWMF awards over $1.1 million to Dana-Farber for WM research advancements
body:
Fall 2025
By Cyrena Musset

The International Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia Foundation (IWMF) has taken a significant step forward in combating Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinemia (WM) by awarding four Dana-Farber scientists more than $1.1 million in grants. This generous funding is intended to fuel groundbreaking studies that aim to uncover the mechanisms behind WM development, pinpoint vulnerabilities, and identify novel drug targets.

WM is a rare, slow-growing form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that typically forms in bone marrow. While it can be treated, the disease remains incurable and treatment resistant. Additionally, given its rarity, testing new therapies can be difficult due to the relatively small patient population. The generosity of IWMF will support the work of these Dana-Farber researchers in advancing scientific breakthroughs in WM.

Yoshinobu “Yoshi” Konishi, PhD, is an instructor in the Ghobrial Lab at Dana-Farber and a recipient of the Robert A. Kyle Career Development Award from IWMF. His research focuses on clarifying cell-cell interactions within the bone marrow microenvironment of patients with plasma cell malignancies with a special focus on early precursor stages. Konishi’s work is essential to understanding how these interactions contribute to the progression of WM and other related diseases.

Filip Garbicz, MD, is a researcher and postdoctoral research fellow at Dana-Farber’s Carrasco Lab in the Department of Pathology and is also a recipient of the Robert A. Kyle Career Development Award. He is focused on studying cancer cell-intrinsic and microenvironmental roles of MYD88 mutations and chromosome 6q deletion in mature B-cell malignancies, with special focus on WM.

His research aims to unravel the genetic complexities that drive WM, potentially leading to targeted therapies that address these specific mutations.

Maria Luisa Guerrera, MD, is a hematologist in Dana-Farber’s Division of Hematologic Neoplasia. She is studying the genomic events that are responsible for WM disease progression following the acquisition of the MYD88 mutation and investigating ways to halt or reverse WM advancement.

“We are excited to support Dana-Farber’s innovative research and pave the way for new treatment strategies and better outcomes for patients.”

Paul Kitchen, The International Waldenström’s Macroglobulinemia Foundation

Zachary Hunter, PhD, is the Bliss Family Investigator at the Bing Center for Waldenstrom’s Macroglobulinemia where he oversees genomic and bioinformatic efforts. Hunter’s current work concentrates on integrating clinical observations with computational biology to discover new drug targets and to start the processes of bringing personalized medicine to patients with WM.

“Since the beginning, the IWMF has sought to raise awareness about Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia and find better treatments for this complex disease,” said IWMF Board Chair Paul Kitchen. “We are excited to support Dana-Farber’s innovative research, which aims to deepen our understanding of WM and pave the way for new treatment strategies and better outcomes for patients.”

title: Bill Pomeroy gives the gift of access to patients with blood cancers
body:
Fall 2025
By Elyse Pleickhardt

In 2004, when William “Bill” Pomeroy was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a fast-growing blood and bone marrow cancer, his future was uncertain.

At that time, it was difficult for older adults with blood cancers to access stem cell transplants, despite the median age of diagnosis being 68. Transplants were typically reserved for those age 35 and younger, and even when an older patient did receive one, the risk of complications was much higher.

But in May 2005, Pomeroy got the fortunate news that a stem cell donor match had been found, and, before he knew it, he was on his way to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute for his transplant.

After his successful transplant, Pomeroy was inspired to help create better outcomes for patients like him. In 2005, he founded the William G. Pomeroy Foundation® to raise awareness and fund initiatives to improve access to blood cancer care. Pomeroy and his foundation have since made gifts totaling more than $1 million to Dana-Farber, supporting research and clinical trials that continue to make leaps and bounds toward more successful transplants.

“Over the past two decades, I have been proud to support Dana-Farber’s lifesaving mission through philanthropy,” said Pomeroy. “Giving back is my way of ensuring that others receive the same opportunity I was so fortunate to experience and to bring hope to patients facing some of life’s toughest challenges. None of us got to where we are on our own.”

Thanks to Pomeroy’s efforts, Dana-Farber has extended stem cell transplant treatment to people into their 70s and 80s and developed new ways of preparing people for transplants so they have better outcomes. Because access to treatment is so important to Pomeroy, one of his recent gifts supports the work of Coleman Lindsley, MD, PhD, whose Stem Cell Donor Registry Study has the potential to redefine how donors are selected for transplant and increase accessibility of this lifesaving treatment.

“This research paves the way for more effective and equitable treatment by exploring donor characteristics beyond age and antigen matching,” Pomeroy said. “Every gift, large or small, helps shape a healthier, brighter future for all.”

Pomeroy’s commitment is bringing blood cancer care to a population who, not so long ago, wasn’t eligible for lifesaving treatment. Dana-Farber and all the patients whose lives his generosity touches are forever grateful for the gift of access.

title: Gift from Haroun Family drives critical research for adult patients with Ewing sarcoma
body:
Fall 2025
By Caitlin Henault

When Rob Haroun was diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma, he knew where to go to find the most supportive and innovative care environment: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. After receiving treatment for leukemia years earlier at multiple health care centers, he and his family found that nothing compared to the care and attention he received at Dana-Farber.

“From the reception staff to the care teams, my experience at Dana-Farber has been head and shoulders above the rest,” said Rob. “It is clear that Dana- Farber is full of intelligent, responsive, and dedicated people.”

Grateful for his care team, led by Priscilla Merriam, MD, clinical director of the Sarcoma Center, and hoping to improve treatment options available to patients with Ewing sarcoma, Rob and his wife, Julie, established the Haroun Family Fund with a generous gift of $1 million. Under the leadership of Suzanne George, MD, chief of the Division of Sarcoma, the fund will support innovative research aimed at discovering the next breakthroughs in treating Ewing sarcoma in adults.

“It is clear that Dana-Farber is full of intelligent, responsive, and dedicated people.”

Rob Haroun

“Due to their rarity, sarcomas receive minimal support from external funding sources, slowing scientific progress and limiting treatments currently available to patients—especially adults who are diagnosed with cancers typically seen and studied in children,” said George. “Philanthropic support from visionary donors like the Harouns is critical to bringing better treatments to patients with these rare diseases.”

The first portion of the Haroun family’s gift will support the efforts of George Demetri, MD, senior vice president for Experimental Therapeutics and the Quick Family Chair in Medical Oncology at Dana-Farber, to test a promising new drug candidate that targets a protein unique to Ewing sarcoma. The second portion will fund innovative research initiatives focused on Ewing sarcoma—chosen through an internal grant proposal process—led by Francesca Alvarez Calderon, MD, PhD; Ryan Collins, PhD; Alan D’Andrea, MD, director of the Susan F. Smith Center for Women’s Cancers, director of the Center for DNA Damage and Repair; and Riaz Gillani, MD.

“Julie and I have been very blessed in our lives—I wouldn’t change anything even if it meant being disease free,” said Rob. “While a cure is the ultimate goal post that drives this gift, any research that slows the disease and puts it into remission would be transformational.”

Added Julie, “our commitment to this research is personal, but we find comfort in the fact that it will benefit so many patients who are facing Ewing sarcoma and other rare cancers.”

title: Donor bequeaths $1 million gift to metastatic breast cancer research
body:
Fall 2025
By Robbie Merritt

Through an estate provision added to her will, Anne P. Olsen has bequeathed $1 million to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. The gift will be directed to the Hilary J. Olsen Fund for Metastatic Breast Cancer, which was established in 2019 by Anne’s son, Jeff. The fund is in memory of Jeff’s late wife Hilary, who was treated twice for metastatic breast cancer (MBC) at Dana-Farber.

Anne’s generous gift, prompted by her daughter-in-law’s diagnosis as well as the diagnosis of her mother, sister, and grandmother all with breast cancer, will support the research of Erica L. Mayer, MD, MPH, director of breast cancer clinical research at Dana-Farber. Mayer cared for Hilary from the time of her breast cancer recurrence in 2015 until her passing in November 2018.

“Cancer is a disease that has affected my whole family, so it feels good to give back,” Anne said. “With metastatic cancers especially, funding for research and testing is so important to be able to understand the unique profile of each patient’s cancer and select the best therapies for them.”

“You hear more stories today than ever before of people surviving for years with metastatic cancers, so it’s a hopeful area, but it has a long way to go,” added Anne’s son, Jeff. “You can see changes in results every day, and it’s important to continue that momentum.”
Through the Olsen Fund, Anne’s bequest will bolster critical care and research for MBC patients at Dana-Farber, including clinical trials and fellowship opportunities, and support Mayer’s research on understanding tumor biology and investigating novel targeted therapies that may shape the future of breast cancer care.

“Not only am I grateful for these funds, which will help drive forward critical work in the breast cancer space, but I am also so heartened that this fund will continue to keep Hilary’s legacy alive,” said Mayer. “Hilary was such a special person, with enormous kindness, enthusiasm, humor, and an incredible ability to support everyone around her. I was so honored to care for her and to meet her amazing family.”

As part of her $1 million bequest, Anne has committed to making annual gifts to the Olsen Fund through her son Jeff’s participation in the Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), the sum of which will be credited toward her bequest. Jeff rides in the PMC as captain of Team Bunger’s Bikers and directs his fundraising to the Olsen Fund. He has participated in the annual two-day bike-a-thon since 2008.
