title: Prostate Cancer Foundation fuels Dana-Farber innovation with $1M+ in grants
body:
Fall 2025
By Casey Reis

For more than 30 years, the Prostate Cancer Foundation (PCF) has been at the forefront of prostate cancer research, funding revolutionary studies and fostering collaboration among physician-scientists. PCF recently awarded $1,050,000 to three Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers through two Young Investigator Awards and one Challenge Award, each supporting research projects aimed at combating prostate cancer and improving outcomes for patients. The grants underscore PCF’s longstanding commitment to advancing transformational research and nurturing the next generation of leaders in the field.

Sylvan Baca, MD, PhD, is the recipient of the 2024 American Cancer Society-PCF Young Investigator Award, a grant designed to support promising early career scientists who are poised to make notable achievements in prostate cancer research. Baca’s team developed a novel platform for liquid biopsies—or blood tests that evaluate cancer on a molecular level rather than with invasive tumor biopsies—monitoring changes in cancer from patient plasma. If successful, the project will assist in disease monitoring, the evaluation of treatment response, and guiding therapy.

Martin Bakht, PhD, has been honored with the 2024 Michael and Lori Milken Family Foundation-PCF Young Investigator Award to support research on metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and mechanisms of resistance to the targeted therapy currently used for treatment. The goal is to gain new insights that will lead to developing strategies for overcoming resistance and improving patient outcomes.

A cross-disciplinary team led by Alan D’Andrea, MD, has received a 2024 PCF Challenge Award for work aiming to refine combination therapies, inhibiting certain pathways to prevent cancer cells from repairing their DNA. D’Andrea’s lab is studying new uses for a drug called novobiocin (NVB) and is collaborating with the National Cancer Institute to test NVB in clinical trials, testing it on its own and in combination with other drugs to evaluate its efficacy and expand upon the understanding and treatment of prostate cancer.

PCF’s generosity not only supports cutting-edge research but also reinforces its dedication to advancing innovation.

“We are honored to support the talented physician-scientists at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute by investing in these promising projects,” said PCF President and CEO Gina B. Carithers. “Together, the PCF and Dana-Farber are paving the way for breakthroughs that could transform the landscape of prostate cancer treatment and improve outcomes for patients worldwide.”

title: The Kesslers’ vision for advancing AML research
body:
Fall 2025
By Lucy McDonald

Distinguished Trustee Michele Kessler and her husband Howard have long stood as pillars of innovation and philanthropy, consistently championing medical research and initiatives that drive advancements in cancer care. Their commitment to these causes is rooted in a profound belief in the power of collaboration. “In my opinion, I think there is a cure. If everyone collaborated like the Manhattan Project, in two or three years, we could solve it. We need people to have that same intention,” Howard said, reflecting on his unwavering belief in a collective effort to defy cancer. A visionary in both business and civic spheres, Howard is no stranger to transformative endeavors.

The Kesslers have been steadfast leaders in Dana-Farber’s philanthropic community. Michele, who became a Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Trustee in 2000, has consistently supported the Institute’s mission through her leadership of various events and campaigns. Their relationship with Dana-Farber deepened when Howard began receiving treatment for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This personal connection has only strengthened their commitment to support cancer research and treatment.

Howard’s approach to tackling complex and challenging causes is marked by determination and a straightforward, guiding principle: “I want to make a difference by creating alternative solutions,” he said of his goal. “Helping people realize what we can do to overcome cancer.” His passion for finding solutions for people with cancer is matched only by his admiration for his wife of 55 years, Michele. “She gave me confidence. She made all the difference in my life,” he shared, highlighting the personal support that fuels his philanthropic spirit.

In a recent demonstration of their enduring generosity, the Kesslers donated $1 million to advance AML research led by Robert Soiffer, MD, chief of the Division of Hematologic Malignancies and Worthington and Margaret Collette Professor of Medicine in the Field of Hematologic Oncology at Harvard Medical School. This substantial gift will empower Soiffer and his team to continue their vital work pursuing personalized approaches to optimize donor cell efficiency, which is crucial in AML treatment. With this funding, Soiffer is poised to leverage findings from previous clinical trials and investigate how new techniques could be applied to AML treatment. Together, these methods represent the most comprehensive approach to enhance transplant success and improve patient outcomes.

This gift embodies a shared vision between Soiffer and the Kesslers: working together leads to innovative solutions. The support not only enhances the potential for groundbreaking discoveries but also reinforces the importance of fostering collaboration to provide a rich foundation for future research. As a result, the future of AML treatment looks brighter, offering renewed hope to patients and families around the world.

title: The Donahues drive research into liquid biopsy for early detection and personalized medicine
body:
Fall 2025
By Michael Quinn

Team science fueled by philanthropy has always provided a driving force for Dana-Farber’s progress against cancer. As loyal Institute supporters, Digger and Susan Donahue play an integral role in this team effort and continually step forward to elevate it.

Recently, Digger and Susan made a generous gift of $1 million to the Donahue Family Fund for Prostate Cancer and the Donahue Family Fund for Cancer Interception at Dana-Farber. Their gift accelerates research to advance a novel liquid biopsy led by Toni Choueiri, MD, director of Dana-Farber’s Lank Center for Genitourinary Oncology and the Jerome and Nancy Kohlberg Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School; and Matthew Freedman, MD, the David Goldstein Chair at Dana-Farber.

Launched with the help of the Donahues’ initial gift to the project in 2020, this first-of-its-kind biopsy leverages the power of epigenetics to uncover tumor biology and ultimately inform treatment decisions. While genetic changes involve variations to the DNA sequence itself, epigenetic changes affect which genes are “expressed”—meaning turned on or off like a light switch—including genes implicated in cancer development and therapeutic resistance. By analyzing tumor-derived DNA fragments in the blood and urine to detect these chemical changes, the biopsy determines what type of cancer a patient has, which therapies the disease might respond to, and whether it is resistant to a particular drug. As a result, the test advances personalized cancer medicine that maximizes efficacy and minimizes side effects. Additionally, the liquid biopsy has the future aim of increasing patient access to potentially lifesaving early detection by providing an upgraded procedure that is less expensive, time-intensive, and invasive than a physical tissue biopsy.

With the Donahues’ sustained investment, Institute investigators were able to enhance and expand the biopsy, which was initially focused on prostate cancer, to address 14 different malignancies, including bladder, colon, lung, and skin cancers. According to Choueiri, such progress demonstrates the importance of the Donahues’ encouragement and impact of their philanthropy. “It means so much to count on Digger’s and Susan’s continued partnership,” he said. “Because of them, our multidisciplinary team can improve this test and bring it to clinics more quickly so it benefits patients everywhere.”

The Donahues are committed to supporting Dana-Farber’s team because they believe in the potential impact of the liquid biopsy. “A less invasive biopsy technique represents a real game-changer,” said Digger. “This test will provide an exciting opportunity for earlier diagnoses of cancers to save more lives,” Susan said. “We’re pleased to see so much progress and glad to be a part of it.”

title: BRCA gene mutations are focus of $1 million research fund
body:
Fall 2025
By Kathy Clute

Between them, Wayland resident Donna Hale and her sister Nancy have been successfully treated for cancer five times. They were more susceptible to the disease because of a mutation in one of their BRCA genes. Mutations in BRCA1 and/or BRCA2 increase the risk of developing certain cancers, particularly of the breast, ovaries, pancreas, and prostate.

When Donna’s breast cancer was first discovered in 1999, routine testing for mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes was not common. But after Nancy got breast cancer five years later and then was diagnosed with lung cancer in 2019, she underwent testing that revealed the genetic vulnerability. Donna immediately got genetic testing as well.

“I tell my sister that she really saved my life,” said Donna, a longtime Dana-Farber supporter along with her husband, John Donovan. “If she hadn’t had lung cancer, I would not have been tested, and they wouldn’t have found my ovarian cancer.” That cancer was discovered only when she underwent preventative surgery to remove her reproductive organs in 2020.

In gratitude for the care Donna received at Dana-Farber and concerned about possible cuts to the Institute’s federal research funding, she and John donated $1 million earlier this year to establish a research fund in support of The Mellen and Eisenson Family Center for BRCA and Related Genes. It will be managed by Judy Garber, MD, MPH, Susan F. Smith Chair and chief of the Division of Cancer Genetics and Prevention. Garber has been Donna’s breast oncologist.

The money will help revolutionize the treatment of BRCA-driven cancers by supporting three key priorities: development of a blood test to identify ovarian cancer via circulating microRNA (small pieces of genetic material) before symptoms appear; clinical trials of better, more precise treatments for patients with BRCA-related tumors; and research into how to reduce breast cancer risk in women taking hormones to offset menopause symptoms after prophylactic ovary removal.

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes that help repair breaks in DNA, a process that is essential to prevent cells from growing and dividing uncontrollably and forming into tumors. Genetic testing is recommended for individuals with a known history of BRCA-driven tumors, but more than half of all people with BRCA mutations have no family history of cancer. Ovarian cancer, for example, is typically not diagnosed until a late stage because there are no screening tests and early symptoms can easily be mistaken for common conditions.

“BRCA is emblazoned on our frontal lobes because of Donna, Nancy, and our two daughters, so we wanted to support research that would benefit people with the mutations,” said John. “The science is so important, and we were anxious to help fund it.”

It will be managed by Judy Garber, MD, MPH, Susan F. Smith Chair and chief of the Division of Cancer Genetics and Prevention. Garber has been Donna’s breast oncologist.

title: Dana-Farber’s Future Cancer Hospital
body:
Fall 2025
By Tarice Gray

In June, Dana-Farber received the key regulatory approvals needed to advance our plans to build New England’s only dedicated inpatient cancer hospital for adult patients. Owned and operated by Dana-Farber, the Future Cancer Hospital will be an independent cancer facility. A new Dana-Farber cancer hospital—combined with our transformational future clinical collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, a Harvard affiliated academic medical center, and its physician group, Harvard Medical Faculty Physicians—will deliver fully integrated, world-class cancer care in a setting devoted exclusively to healing and hope. It is the right care model for the future of cancer care and will allow us to provide the best care for our patients for years to come. A visionary new facility that will redefine how cancer is treated, the Future Cancer Hospital will offer 450,000 square feet of dedicated patient care space, 300 private inpatient beds—including 30 licensed ICU beds and 16-bed observation suite, and specialized facilities.

Bringing this innovative care model to life depends, in part, on visionary philanthropy. The partnership of our dedicated community of benefactors will make this bold and ambitious vision for the future of cancer care a reality—creating a world where all patients receive integrated, best-in-class inpatient and outpatient care from an exceptional team of clinicians and scientists focused solely on cancer. Please visit www.dana-farber.org/about/our-vision-for-the-future-of-cancer-care for more information.

title: AACR grants support sarcoma, renal cell carcinoma, and cancer biology research
body:
Fall 2025
By Cyrena Musset

The American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) recently awarded $580,000 to three Dana-Farber physician-scientists who are investigating new methods of prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of various types of cancers. As the first cancer research organization dedicated to preventing and curing cancer, AACR is a long-standing partner in Dana-Farber’s mission to defy cancer.

Erica Pimenta, MD, PhD, Medical Oncology Fellow, is clinically and scientifically focused on sarcoma, which develops in bone and connective tissue. Her work involves studying pathogenesis and immune evasion, leveraging both computational and molecular biology approaches.

“I am extremely grateful and honored to be awarded the AACR-QuadW Foundation Sarcoma Research Fellowship in Memory of Willie Tichenor,” said Pimenta. “As a sarcoma-focused physician-scientist, I can assure patients that sarcoma research is active and advanced. This award supports the continuation of vital work, providing protected research time for excellence in biologic discovery. Thank you to all who made this possible.”

Cary Weiss, MD, PhD, Pediatric Hematology/Oncology Fellow, studies translocation renal cell carcinoma, a rare and aggressive type of kidney cancer that is more common in children, young people, women, and as a secondary malignancy. He’s working on a new approach using Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras, which are special molecules designed to break down harmful proteins quickly and completely.

“I am thrilled to be awarded the AACR-Exelixis Renal Cell Carcinoma Research Fellowship, which provides essential funding to advance my research on translocation renal cell carcinoma and supports my development as an independent physician-scientist,” said Weiss. “This opportunity significantly contributes to my goal of improving outcomes for pediatric and adolescent/young adult cancer patients.”

Dana-Farber researcher, Nika Danial, PhD, in collaboration with Jarrod Marto, PhD and Mariella Filbin, MD, PhD, are researching histone mutant diffuse midline gliomas, a type of brain tumor caused by certain cells that should develop into glial cells but instead stay in an immature “stem-like” state.

“This award will catalyze high-risk, high-reward studies that could lead to significant breakthroughs in understanding how certain lipid-protein interactions affect glioma, an untapped area of discovery in metabolic signaling,” said Danial. “The findings could also impact our understanding of other cancers where cell development is disrupted or stalled.”

title: Cookies for Kids’ Cancer funds groundbreaking Dana-Farber pediatric cancer research
body:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

Cookies for Kids’ Cancer has awarded two grants totaling $600,000 to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute to support groundbreaking pediatric cancer research. The funding supports two projects: one led by A. Thomas Look, MD, focused on high-risk neuroblastoma, and another led by Scott Armstrong, MD, PhD, targeting a rare and aggressive form of childhood leukemia. This is part of their ongoing commitment, having previously funded more than $2.6 million in pediatric cancer research grants to Dana-Farber through a rigorous peer-reviewed process.

Look received a $300,000 grant in 2025 to advance treatments for children with high-risk neuroblastoma. These patients often endure a year of intensive treatment followed by post-consolidation therapy, which includes isotretinoin and an anti-GD2 antibody. While this regimen improves survival, many children relapse due to treatment limitations. Look’s research arose from a screen that identified a drug, PF-9363, which works synergistically with isotretinoin to extend suppression of cancer cell growth and increase the expression of GD2, making neuroblastoma cells more vulnerable to immunotherapy that specifically targets this cell surface glycolipid. This combination therapy significantly improved the killing of human neuroblastoma cells growing in immunosuppressed mice and was well tolerated. His team is now testing a three-drug regimen—including PF-9363, isotretinoin, and the anti-GD2 antibody—in this model system to validate a treatment schedule suitable for testing to improve outcomes for children with neuroblastoma. If successful, this could lead to clinical trials and offer new hope for children with treatment-resistant neuroblastoma.

“There’s a critical need to develop smarter, more targeted treatments for these children,” Armstrong said. “Our goal is to bring therapies to the clinic that directly address the biology of their disease and improve their chances of survival.”

Scott Armstrong, MD, PhD, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute

Cookies for Kids’ Cancer awarded Armstrong a $300,000 grant in 2024 to study childhood leukemia with NUP98 gene rearrangements, which are associated with poor outcomes and limited treatment options. His team is targeting the Menin-KMT2A complex, a key driver of leukemia gene expression, and exploring a second target, KAT6A, for combination therapy.

“There’s a critical need to develop smarter, more targeted treatments for these children,” Armstrong said. “Our goal is to bring therapies to the clinic that directly address the biology of their disease and improve their chances of survival.”

Thanks to funding from Cookies for Kids’ Cancer and the revolutionary work of two Dana-Farber researchers, these studies represent a significant step toward better outcomes for children with some of the most challenging pediatric cancers.

title: Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation helps advance glioblastoma research
body:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

The Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation has awarded $524,081 to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute to advance novel immunotherapy approaches to treat glioblastoma. This funding supports a project focused on a novel treatment strategy for glioblastoma led by David Reardon, MD, Clinical Director of the Center for Neuro-Oncology and Alperin Family Chair in Neuro-Oncology at Dana-Farber.

Glioblastoma is an aggressive brain cancer with limited treatment options and a median survival of just 15 months. Most patients experience tumor recurrence, and few therapies offer meaningful benefit after relapse. Unlike other cancers that respond well to immunotherapy, glioblastoma has proven resistant due to its “cold” tumor environment. This “cold” tumor environment lacks immune cell activity and actively suppresses immune responses.

CUE-102, an investigational drug, aims to overcome this barrier. It is designed to activate and expand the body’s own cancer-fighting T cells that target a protein called Wilms Tumor 1 (WT1), which is expressed in nearly all glioblastomas. Because it works in the bloodstream and lymph nodes—rather than needing to cross into the brain—CUE-102 primes the immune system to recognize and destroy tumor cells.

“Glioblastoma has long resisted the kinds of immune-based treatments that have transformed care for other cancers,” said Reardon. “CUE-102 represents a novel strategy to awaken the immune system and direct it against a target commonly found in these tumors.”

Early clinical trial results with CUE-102 for other cancers are promising: the treatment appears safe, with mostly mild side effects, and nearly half of all patients experienced disease control. Importantly, the study confirmed that CUE-102 successfully activated the targeted immune cells.

“Glioblastoma has long resisted the kinds of immune-based treatments that have transformed care for other cancers,” said Reardon. “CUE-102 represents a novel strategy to awaken the immune system and direct it against a target commonly found in these tumors.”

David Reardon, MD, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute

This work represents a critical step forward in addressing one of the most challenging cancers. It is made possible through the generous support of the Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation, whose dedication to cancer research is helping to drive innovation and hope.

title: METAvivor advances metastatic breast cancer research
body:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

METAvivor has awarded three grants totaling $850,000 to advance metastatic breast cancer research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. More than half of this funding—$450,000—supports a project led by Rinath Jeselsohn, MD, which aims to develop a clinically accessible tool to help physicians predict which patients with advanced hormone receptor-positive breast cancer will respond to a common treatment combination. By analyzing routine clinical and tumor data, the tool—based on a machine learning algorithm—aims to guide more personalized treatment choices and reduce exposure to less effective therapies. The study will also explore how the immune environment of tumors may contribute to treatment resistance.

The remaining two grants of $200,000 each support early career investigators Stefania Morganti, MD, and Paolo Tarantino, MD, PhD. Morganti is investing the role of minimal residual disease via circulating tumor DNA in patients with HER2+ metastatic breast cancer (MBC) and exceptional response to therapy. Tarantino’s research focuses on innovating and refining methods to predict responses to antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) therapies in patients with advanced breast cancer. Tarantino said, “Antibody-Drug Conjugates have had a transformative impact on the prognosis of MBC, but we’re still unable to adequately tailor their use. With the critical support of METAvivor, we plan to leverage cutting-edge technologies to learn from our patients’ samples and develop biomarkers for precision ADC treatment”

Kelly Shanahan, MD, President of METAvivor, emphasizes the organization’s commitment. She said, “METAvivor funds the best in research focused on people whose breast cancer has already metastasized, which is why nine Dana-Farber investigators have been awarded METAvivor research awards since 2019, more than any other institution. As someone living with MBC, I am grateful for the brilliant minds at Dana Farber who are developing treatments that will help me and people like me live longer and better.”

“METAvivor funds the best in research focused on people whose breast cancer has already metastasized, which is why nine Dana-Farber investigators have been awarded METAvivor research awards since 2019, more than any other institution. As someone living with MBC, I am grateful for the brilliant minds at Dana Farber who are developing treatments that will help me and people like me live longer and better.”

Kelly Shanahan, MD, President of METAvivor

Through these grants, METAvivor continues to make a significant impact on MBC, fostering advancements that promise to improve patient outcomes and extend lives.

title: Massachusetts Life Sciences Center fuels advances in immunotherapy and workforce development
body:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

Dana-Farber Cancer Institute has received nearly $800,000 in support from the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center (MLSC) to advance cancer research and workforce development. This funding supports two pivotal initiatives focused on access and equity: the Continuing Umbrella Research Experiences (CURE) Program and a groundbreaking project in novel therapeutics delivery.

Eric Smith, MD, PhD received a $750,000 grant for his work in novel therapeutics delivery. Working in partnership with Massachusetts clinical-stage biotechnology company, Strand Therapeutics, the team, which includes a postdoc hired specifically for this project, has been working together to optimize an RNA approach for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) delivery in patients, aiming to transform cancer immunotherapy. Such an approach could circumvent the resource-intensive manufacturing processes deployed in current CAR therapies, thereby making advanced CAR therapies more accessible to underserved populations and patients with rare cancers. The project promises to enhance accessibility, speed, and efficacy of treatment, offering hope to those who lack access to tertiary care centers.

Kirk Taylor, MD, President and CEO of MLSC, said, “If successful, this project will revolutionize cancer treatment accessibility, offering rapid and cost-effective solutions to patients in need. We are proud to support Dana-Farber’s innovative work that aligns with our mission to advance life sciences and improve patient outcomes.”

The MLSC Novel Therapeutics Delivery program fosters collaboration across engineering, biology, chemistry, and medicine, addressing complex challenges in therapeutic delivery. With this funding, Dana-Farber is poised to make significant strides in cancer research, offering hope to patients and communities worldwide.

“If successful, this project will revolutionize cancer treatment accessibility, offering rapid and cost-effective solutions to patients in need. We are proud to support Dana-Farber’s innovative work that aligns with our mission to advance life sciences and improve patient outcomes.”

Kirk Taylor, MD, President and CEO of MLSC

Karen Burns White, deputy associate director of Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center Community Engagement and Outreach, received more than $43,000 for the 2024 CURE Program. This initiative provides student intern stipends, fostering the next generation of researchers committed to health equity and reducing the inequitable burden of cancer. Burns White emphasizes the importance of early exposure and engagement to all levels of cancer research and care. MLSC has been a dedicated partner to the CURE Program, broadening opportunities for students across Massachusetts and helping to ensure a future healthcare workforce of well-prepared, highly skilled, and diverse candidates. The MLSC has provided over $130,000 to support a total of 37 internships since 2018.

title: Rally Foundation supports bold pediatric cancer research
body:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

Rally Foundation for Childhood Cancer Research recently awarded $450,000 in grants to four Dana-Farber researchers developing innovative treatments for pediatric cancer. Recipients include Tom Rosenberg, MD; James Morrow, MD, PhD; Basudev Chowdhury, PhD; and Yana Pikman, MD.

Rosenberg is designing new therapies for children with recurrent atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor (ATRT), a rare and aggressive brain cancer that primarily affects infants. While current treatments cure nearly half of patients with ATRT, there are no effective therapies for patients whose disease recurs. In addition, the intensive therapy patients receive often causes significant long-term side effects. Rosenberg designed a platform study that will test safer, more targeted therapies.

Morrow is studying osteosarcoma, a bone cancer common in adolescents and young adults. Recent work has identified two tumor subtypes—one that resembles normal bone and responds well to treatment and another that behaves more like stem cells and spreads aggressively. Morrow is testing whether the latter can be reprogrammed into bone-like cells to improve outcomes. “Understanding what makes these tumors more aggressive may open the door to entirely new treatment strategies,” said Morrow.

Chowdhury is investigating the biology of pediatric leukemias, including acute lymphoblastic leukemia and acute myeloid leukemia. By studying molecular vulnerabilities in these cancers, his research could uncover new targets for treatment and lead to breakthrough therapies.

“Understanding what makes these tumors more aggressive could open the door to entirely new treatment strategies.”

James Morrow, MD, PhD

Pikman led the first national precision medicine trial using genomic testing to guide treatment for children with high-risk, relapsed, or treatment-resistant leukemia. She is now expanding this work to pediatric centers across the Northeast to assess how genomic testing impacts diagnosis and treatment of pediatric leukemia and testing the feasibility of offering extended genomic testing at the regional level. Her research seeks to improve access to testing, support clinicians in using genomic data, and ultimately reduce toxicity of treatment while improving survival.

These early stage, high potential studies represent Rally Foundation’s commitment to funding research that improves both outcomes and quality of life for children with cancer.

title: Inspiring hope: Catherine’s journey and the impact of Giving Day
body:
Fall 2025
By Hannah White Hannah

Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Jimmy Fund’s annual Giving Day, held on Wednesday, May 21 this year, united patients, families, employees, and supporters worldwide in giving to Dana-Farber’s mission to defy cancer. All donations supporting Giving Day were tripled-matched to fuel groundbreaking research and compassionate care, thanks to a generous $250,000 gift from an anonymous Dana-Farber Trustee. During this Giving Day, over $832,000 was raised, surpassing the goal of $500,000 in unrestricted funds, with 94% of the total being unrestricted. This funding is crucial as it provides researchers the flexibility to pursue innovative treatments and breakthroughs at a rapid pace. Patients like Catherine benefit directly from the lifesaving research and care made possible through Giving Day.

Catherine’s journey with cancer began unexpectedly while living abroad in Geneva, Switzerland. At 30 weeks pregnant, she discovered a lump on her chest, initially dismissing it as a pregnancy-related issue. Her diagnosis of stage II triple-negative breast cancer came as a shock.

Faced with the daunting reality of cancer during pregnancy, Catherine found hope at Dana-Farber. “When I found out that Dana-Farber has a program specifically for patients diagnosed with cancer while pregnant, I felt a sense of relief,” she said. Under the care of Ann Partridge, MD, MPH, the Eric P. Winer, MD, Chair in Breast Cancer Research at Dana-Farber, Catherine embarked on a comprehensive treatment plan. “The care I have received at Dana-Farber has been nothing short of amazing,” she shared. Today, Catherine is grateful to Dana-Farber for the support that allows her to focus on her health and her family, including her newborn daughter, Camila, who was delivered safely and is perfectly healthy.

The success of Giving Day is a testament to the power of community. With the community’s support on Giving Day and every day, Dana-Farber maintains its momentum, ensuring we are there for every patient who walks through our doors.

title: Honoring whole blood and platelet donors
body:
Fall 2025
By Lori Dougherty
Photography by John Deputy

As much as any drug or technology, whole blood and platelets are lifesaving resources for cancer patients. The Kraft Family Blood Donor Center celebrates the compassionate individuals who give so generously at the center’s annual Breakfast of Champions. Sunday, Apr. 6 marked the 41st anniversary of the Kraft Family Blood Donor Center. Institute Trustee Dan Kraft welcomed 225 whole blood and platelet donors and guests to Gillette Stadium to celebrate 5,053 units of platelets, 7,516 units of whole blood, and 480 stem cell products they donated in the prior year. The donations made a powerful difference in the lives of 14,317 patients and their families.

title: Ning Zhao & Ge Li Family Initiative in Nursing
body:
Fall 2025
By Lori Dougherty
Photography by Sasha Pedro

On May 5, the Institute celebrated Anne Gross, PhD, RN, NEA-BC, FAAN, the inaugural incumbent of the Ning Zhao Chair of Nursing at Dana-Farber. As Senior Vice President for Patient Care Services and Chief Nursing Officer, Gross led the achievement of two consecutive Magnet® designations for excellence in nursing; improved patient access to and the quality and safety of oncology care; and developed programs to build the oncology nursing workforce and advance nursing science.

On the same day, Dana-Farber celebrated the opening of the Ning Zhao & Ge Li Nursing Simulation Center, which offers a training environment where nurses, clinical assistants, oncology nurse navigators, and other staff can develop and refine essential clinical skills. The Simulation Center, the chair, and a scholarship fund for clinical assistants are made possible by the Ning Zhao & Ge Li Family Initiative in Nursing, representing the largest single gift to nursing in the Institute’s history.

title: A Message from Melany Duval
body:
Fall 2025

Dear Friends,

Science has long been the catalyst for transformative cancer care. More recently, we’ve witnessed revolutionary advances that have benefited patients and those who hold them dear.

In my time working with this community of generous donors, I have come to realize how deeply you understand and appreciate the immense value of scientific research. That is why your support is so impactful and continues to serve as a bedrock of hope for Dana-Farber—especially now as we navigate the unsteady reality caused by federal policy that impacts research funding. We are assured by your investment in scientific discovery that supports all aspects of cancer treatment and care. In the following pages are stories of incredible philanthropy that has enabled prevention and early detection, as well as groundbreaking treatments and accelerated scientific breakthroughs. You play a vital role in shaping a community that champions science as the foundation of every solution.

Our community includes tremendous donors and volunteers. One example featured in this issue is the Dana-Farber Marathon Challenge (DFMC), which is singularly focused on elevating the importance of basic science. Comprised of volunteer runners and fundraisers, the DFMC hosted roughly 500 runners from across the country and the world for the 129th Boston Marathon®, with a goal of raising over $8 million for the Claudia Adams Barr Program in Innovative Basic Cancer Research. Basic science is a critical element of Dana-Farber’s unique commitment to research and clinical care propelled by support from our generous donor community.

As this issue goes to press, Dr. Ben Ebert will have completed his first year as President and CEO of Dana-Farber. In this inaugural year, Dr. Ebert, a world-renowned medical oncologist and researcher, has elevated our commitment to scientific research, and alongside our donors, is further advancing opportunities for more preventive treatments and promising cancer care options. His plan for an even more innovative and collaborative Dana-Farber is grounded in the support of our generous donor community. It is because of you that the work of our mission continues—bolder than ever before.

With deep appreciation,

Melany N. Duval
Senior Vice President and Chief Philanthropy Officer

title: Janower family drives pediatric brain tumor research forward
photo_credit: Photography by Rick Bern, Craig Orsini
body:
Summer 2025
By Cyrena Musset
Photography by Rick Bern, Craig Orsini

Cindy and AJ Janower’s introduction to the challenging world of childhood cancer began when their daughter, Samantha “Sammi,” was just three years old. A casual remark from their babysitter about Sammi’s limited use of her right side led to a life-altering discovery. Sammi, now 24, was diagnosed with a pediatric brain tumor, and began treatment at the Dana-Farber Jimmy Fund Clinic. Her mother, Cindy, remembered: “It was a truly scary moment when we first understood our daughter had a life-threatening disease with no known cure.”

“Pediatric brain tumors were a classic orphan disease with limited researcher interest due to limited funding for new drug development,” AJ recalled. “We decided to raise money for early stage research to break this doom loop.” Their efforts, alongside several other similarly situated families, led to the creation of the Dana-Farber Pediatric Low-Grade Astrocytoma (PLGA) Program, the world’s first multi-disciplinary program focused on research for these types of brain tumors. Harnessing Dana-Farber’s expertise, this program was pivotal in the identification, development, and FDA approval of tovorafenib (Ojemda), the first-ever systemic therapy for BRAF-rearranged pediatric low-grade gliomas.

“These families raised the money to fund the research which led to a new FDA-approved drug,” Pratiti “Mimi” Bandopadhayay, MBBS, PhD, a pediatric neuro-oncologist at Dana-Farber and the director of the Dana-Farber PLGA Program, said with pride. “As a result of these efforts, children all over the world will benefit from meaningfully improved outcomes and higher quality of life.”


The Janower family’s dedication to the Institute spans the two decades since Sammi’s initial diagnosis, including multiple research grants and capital campaign commitments, as well as AJ’s appointment as a Dana-Farber Trustee in 2015. Additionally, AJ has been a tireless fundraiser and is poised for a 17th riding in the Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), the nation’s single most successful athletic fundraising event and Dana-Farber’s largest contributor, accounting for 66% of the Jimmy Fund’s annual revenue.

Sammi first joined AJ in the PMC when she was just 15, becoming the youngest participant that year to complete the full two-day ride. “Sammi was not physically able to ride on her own, so we did it together on a tandem bike,” AJ said.

“She was our photographer, social media director, and DJ. Occasionally, she even pedaled!” This summer Sammi will ride in her 10th PMC, providing inspiration for a cadre of dear friends on Team Samantha and other teams who dedicate their funds to pediatric brain tumor research.

“Thanks to the Janower family’s ongoing support, the PLGA Program has made amazing progress for patients and families,” Bandopadhayay said. “Their contributions will continue to help us explore new ways to target these tumors, train the next generation of scientists, and keep our cutting-edge equipment up to date. I am very grateful for their partnership in this important work.” To ensure continued long-term progress, Cindy and AJ recently made a seven-figure bequest to advance pediatric brain tumor research at Dana-Farber. Planned gifts like bequests ensure critical future support that will sustain Dana-Farber’s mission in the decades to come.

“I feel tremendous gratitude for all of my caregivers at the Jimmy Fund Clinic; I know how fortunate I am to have a world-class team at my side. I’m also deeply proud of the Dana-Farber researchers, and our own small contribution to supporting them, to improve the prognosis for other similarly situated kids in the future.”

Sammi Janower, cancer survivor


Reflecting on her cancer journey, Sammi shared, “I feel tremendous gratitude for all of my caregivers at the Jimmy Fund Clinic; I know how fortunate I am to have a world-class team at my side. I’m also deeply proud of the Dana-Farber researchers, and our own small contribution to supporting them, to improve the prognosis for other similarly situated kids in the future.”

title: Collaboration catalyst: Unique gift builds culture ahead of historic partnership
photo_credit: Photography by Sasha Pedro, Michael Blanchard
body:
Summer 2025
By Katie Berger
Photography by Sasha Pedro, Michael Blanchard

Randi and Joel Cutler couldn’t agree more with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) President Peter J. Healy’s familiar statement: “In partnerships, culture beats strategy every time.” This was their first thought upon learning of the early plans for what would become the future Dana-Farber Beth Israel Deaconess Cancer Collaboration (Collaboration). “The concept is brilliant, between two world-class organizations,” said Joel. “It’s a hand-in-glove partnership.”

“The concept is brilliant, between two world-class organizations. it’s a hand-in-glove partnership.”

Joel Cutler

So, they set about structuring a $2 million gift to be shared equally between Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and BIDMC—the first-ever joint gift in support of the two Harvard teaching institutions. The Cutlers established the Culture and Collaboration Initiative with the goal to build on existing goodwill and intensify the already strong, dual leadership dynamic, and expand this critical mindset to both providers and patients. “From the very first meeting, we were blown away by the leaders involved,” said Randi. “Everyone was in lockstep, and they set the tone.” The couple has graciously hosted events in their Boston and Cape Cod homes, enabling key stakeholders to truly get to know one another on a personal level. And their gift will continue to enable patient, staff and donor engagement activities, learning series, and town hall gatherings.


This gift comes at a pivotal time. Following rigorous evaluation by the Massachusetts Department of Public Health (DPH), including an Independent Cost Analysis commissioned by DPH, showing that the Collaboration would be beneficial to the region, the state’s Public Health Council voted unanimously to approve Dana-Farber’s Determination of Need application for a new dedicated adult inpatient cancer hospital. The Boston Planning and Development Agency Board (BPDA) then voted unanimously to approve the designs for the 300-bed hospital. BPDA’s approval is the culmination of a rigorous project review process and reflects the Collaboration’s tremendous potential to provide lifesaving care to countless patients. While city regulatory reviews are ongoing, the shared vision is to build a 300-bed cancer hospital to be located at One Joslin Place in the Longwood Medical Area solely dedicated to oncology care—the only hospital of its kind in the region. At 10 stories high and spanning 450,000 square feet with 10 inpatient floors, the Future Cancer Hospital would connect the BIDMC and Dana-Farber campuses to provide a seamless patient experience.

Looking to the future, the impact of the Collaboration cannot be overstated—and philanthropy will continue to be vital for both institutions. Like many in our hospital communities, giving back is a responsibility the Cutlers take seriously. “We all believe this hospital, and this collaboration, will provide the gold standard of cancer care,” said Joel, a member of the Board of Trustees at BIDMC. Adds Randi: “The impact will be tremendous because we have two remarkable organizations working tightly together to make it so.”

title: Breast Cancer Research Foundation grants more than $4 million to speed Dana-Farber research
body:
Summer 2025
By Lucy McDonald
Photography by Sam Ogden

For more than 30 years, the Breast Cancer Research Foundation (BCRF) has generously supported the world’s most promising breast cancer research—including longstanding support of groundbreaking work at Dana-Farber. By providing crucial research funding to leaders in the field, BCRF aims to expedite breakthroughs that will change the lives of patients around the world.

“Our goal is singular: rid the world of breast cancer,” said Donna McKay, president and CEO of BCRF. “We are very proud to support cutting-edge research at Dana-Farber that gets us closer to that goal and promises to change the lives of patients and their families.”

Building on their past support of Dana-Farber, BCRF recently made grants totaling more than $4 million to 12 exceptional Institute physician-scientists. Among these, one grant is accelerating the work of Judy Garber, MD, MPH, chief of the Division of Cancer Genetics and Prevention and the Susan F. Smith Chair at Dana-Farber, who is investigating the biology underlying BRCA-associated, ER-positive breast cancers. Garber, who has received support from BCRF for nearly 25 years, was also honored with the prestigious Jill Rose Award in 2024—BCRF’s highest scientific honor—in recognition for her landmark contributions to the field.

Another recent BCRF grant is driving important research by Jennifer Ligibel, MD, director of the Leonard P. Zakim Center for Integrative Therapies and Healthy Living, focused on exploring the link between exercise and breast cancer. While higher levels of physical activity have been linked to lower risk of developing breast cancer, the biological processes underlying this association are not yet understood. Past research led by Ligibel and her colleague Bruce Spiegelman, PhD, director of the Center for Energy Metabolism and Chronic Disease, revealed that a hormone released during exercise called irisin may slow breast cancer development by activating the immune system. Building on her work with Spiegelman, Ligibel is leveraging. BCRF support to measure the effects of irisin on the immune system in laboratory models of non-cancerous breast tissue and models of early breast cancer development. In parallel, she has launched a clinical trial to test the effects of a 12-week exercise program on circulating irisin and immune markers in breast tissue.

By exploring this connection, Ligibel, Spiegelman, and their teams aim to clarify the mechanisms through which exercise can reduce cancer risk and, ultimately, identify new targets for developing drugs that prevent and treat this disease. Their goal is to develop drugs that hold promise for even the most difficult-to-treat forms of breast cancer, changing the lives of patients everywhere.

title: Freedman named to David Goldstein Chair
body:
Summer 2025
By Lori Dougherty
Photography by Sasha Pedro

Matthew Freedman, MD, was named the inaugural incumbent of the David Goldstein Chair at Dana-Farber, endowed by the late Jonathan Goldstein to support kidney cancer research in memory of his father, David Goldstein. Freedman is known for his research on genitourinary cancers and on epigenetics—the study of markers that alter the function of genes and can influence cancer.

In 2023, Freedman and colleagues developed a blood test using innovative liquid biopsy technology, which can reveal if a person has cancer and, if so, how best to treat it. The David Goldstein Chair enables Freedman to continue such collaborations to advance early detection, interception, and treatment of cancer, including kidney cancers.

title: Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation invests in tomorrow’s discoveries
body:
Summer 2025
By Lucy McDonald

Dana-Farber received over $3,156,000 in grants from the Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation in 2024 supporting 10 physician-scientists and researchers. This generous funding is part of the foundation’s decades-long support of Dana-Farber to assist early career investigators in pursuing their research endeavors.
For over 75 years, Damon Runyon has been identifying “brave and bold” early career scientists and providing them with resources to make the next breakthroughs in cancer research. The foundation has invested more than $450 million in nearly 4,000 young scientists nationwide who are engaged in high-risk, high-reward cancer research, encouraging them “to go where others haven’t.” The foundation’s approach not only accelerates the pace of discovery but also inspires a new generation of cancer researchers to push the boundaries of what is possible.
Damon Runyon’s support acknowledges the importance of safeguarding research time for early career investigators at Dana-Farber, who are essential to the “bench to bedside” process of transforming laboratory research into effective clinical treatments. Such funding enables Dana-Farber researchers and physician-scientists to focus on complex scientific questions and collaborate across disciplines, driving breakthroughs that enhance patient care.

The foundation notably honored three female researchers, Megan Insco, MD, PhD; Erin Parry, MD, PhD; and Lachelle Weeks, MD, PhD, with the Damon Runyon Clinical Investigator Award. Each year, this award recognizes physician-scientists who are engaged in disease-focused research characterized by exceptional innovation and creativity, aimed at advancing cancer treatment practices.

“Empowering young researchers fuels innovation and ensures a vibrant future for scientific discovery.”

Yung Lie, PhD, Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation


“Empowering young researchers fuels innovation and ensures a vibrant future for scientific discovery,” said Yung Lie, PhD, president and chief executive officer of the Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation. “Supporting these gifted scientists to explore bold and critical questions in cancer research fills us with pride.”

Damon Runyon also made the following grants in 2024: Physician-Scientist Training Award to Rebecca Zon, MD; Pediatric Cancer Research Fellowships to James Morrow, MD, PhD; Geoffrey Smith, MD, PhD; and Lara Wahlster, MD, PhD; Scholars Program for Advancing Research and Knowledge grant to Katelyn King; Quantitative Biology Fellowship to Ahmed Roman, PhD; and Dale F. Frey Award to Xin Gu, PhD. These grants represent a diverse array of research areas including melanoma, various blood cancers, and osteosarcoma, reflecting the foundation’s holistic strategy to tackle cancer from multiple angles.

title: HomeGoods expands support to enhance patient care
photo_credit: Photography by Sam Ogden, John Deputy
body:
Summer 2025
By Casey Reis
Photography by Sam Ogden, John Deputy

For more than two decades, HomeGoods has fostered hope and healing for families facing cancer, raising critical funds for Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. Through HomeGoods’ Find Home Anywhere mission—funded largely by donations from its generous shoppers—HomeGoods and the TJX Foundation have made a three-year commitment to donate at least $3.6 million to Dana-Farber. This support will help fund key initiatives at the Institute, including the Center for Adolescent and Young Adult Oncology, the Patient Assistance Program, and the Pediatric Resource Program. HomeGoods’ Find Home Anywhere initiative is committed to helping people find a sense of home wherever life takes them.

The center is dedicated to improving outcomes and quality of life for adolescent and young adult (AYA) patients, a demographic facing unique challenges in cancer treatment and survivorship. Under the guidance of co-medical directors Lindsay Frazier, MD, and Ann LaCasce, MD, MMSc, HomeGoods support helps fund research and care specific to AYA patients, addressing medical and psychosocial needs. Efforts include supporting the HomeGoods Young Adult Lounge at Dana-Farber, which opened in 2024. The bright design, welcoming space, and thoughtful construction were developed in collaboration with Dana-Farber faculty, HomeGoods leadership, and patient focus groups. Custom programs include support groups, targeted therapies, décor refreshes, and space makeovers for patients.

The three-year commitment also supports the HomeGoods Adult Housing Assistance Fund, a patient assistance program overseen by Deborah Toffler, MSW, LCSW, senior director of Patient Care Services at Dana-Farber. The fund provides financial aid to adults undergoing treatment, helping to cover expenses like rent and mortgage payments, so patients can focus on care and well-being without the stress of housing instability. Similarly, the HomeGoods Pediatric Housing Assistance Program, led by Pediatric Resource Program Director Joe Chabot, MS, offers financial support to pediatric patients, alleviating housing expenses and aiding families needing temporary lodging or facing relocation costs.


This year marks the 25th anniversary of the Dana-Farber and HomeGoods partnership, through which HomeGoods has helped impact research and care profoundly.

“We are proud of the close collaboration with Dana-Farber over the past 25 years and are grateful to lend a hand in a uniquely HomeGoods way through Find Home Anywhere, helping patients and families feel comforted, welcome, and at home. We’ve accomplished a lot together and are excited for more to come this year and beyond,” said Victoria Shonkoff, senior vice president and marketing director, HomeGoods and Homesense.

title: Dana-Farber’s neuro-inclusive program sets new standard in cancer care
body:
Summer 2025
By Lucy McDonald

At Dana-Farber, we recognize that each cancer diagnosis is as unique as the individual facing it. Whether expected or unexpected, a patient’s diagnosis introduces a series of evolving challenges that vary in complexity and impact on their lives. Personalized support and tailored care is needed to meet each patient’s specific circumstances, especially those that require more than the standard of care.

In March 2024, Dana-Farber launched the Neuro-Inclusive Oncology Care and Empowerment Program to provide specialized cancer care for adults with intellectual and/or developmental disabilities (IDD). Dana-Farber is the first cancer center in the country to establish such a program, addressing the unique needs of this patient population. The establishment of the program was made possible by a combined gift of $2.64 million from the C.J.L. Charitable Foundation and the Nancy Lurie Marks Family Foundation. The program focuses on meeting the needs of patients with IDD that are frequently overlooked in cancer care. Compared to patients who do not have IDD, those with IDD are diagnosed with cancer at later stages, experience delays to their care, are given fewer treatment options, and die from cancer at higher rates. This first-of-its-kind initiative aims to improve outcomes by offering tailored education, supportive relationships, sensory accommodations, and inclusive counseling to patients.

The program is spearheaded by experienced, licensed social workers, including senior program specialist Melissa Levin, MSW, LICSW, who guides its growth and direction. “The program is truly human-centered,” said Levin. “Disability is an important part of oneself. It is intersectional across age, gender, sexual orientation, socioeconomic status, culture. Disability exists in all of those realms. Our program acknowledges that.”

There are many touchpoints and opportunities for referrals within a patient’s journey through treatment. When obstacles or challenges are identified for patients with IDD during initial assessments, social workers can help understand their communication style, language abilities, learning preferences, and information processing methods. Other key interventions include preparing patients for what to expect during appointments, creating strategies and visual aids to ease anxiety about visits, and identifying sensory and/or physical accommodations to enhance the treatment environment.

Now fully integrated within Dana-Farber’s Department of Supportive Oncology and available to patients in all outpatient facilities, this unprecedented program not only addresses the needs of neurodiverse patients but also reinforces Dana-Farber’s dedication to fostering a more inclusive and understanding health care environment for all. The program aspires to be a model for replication and teaching in other major cancer care hospitals, encouraging the widespread adoption of neuro-inclusive practices throughout the healthcare industry.
excerpt: In March 2024, Dana-Farber launched the Neuro-Inclusive Oncology Care and Empowerment Program to provide specialized cancer care for adults with intellectual and/or developmental disabilities (IDD). The establishment of the program was made possible by a combined gift of $2.64 million from the C.J.L. Charitable Foundation and the Nancy Lurie Marks Family Foundation.

title: Defeating treatment-resistant lung cancer
body:
Summer 2025
By Kathleen Clute
Photography by Sam Ogden

A collaborative, multi-institution team led by Dana-Farber’s David Barbie, MD, received a four-year, $2.5 million grant from the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer (IASLC) and Lung Cancer Research Foundation (LCRF) for researching a cure for non-small cell lung carcinoma. Barbie is the director of Dana-Farber’s Lowe Center for Thoracic Oncology Jane Rodgers Chair at Dana-Farber.

While the disease can often be successfully treated in the short term, the cancer cells eventually become resistant to chemotherapy and other therapies. One reason is drug-tolerant resister (DTP) cells that hide from both cancer treatments and the immune system, allowing the cancer to return and spread. Barbie’s team is searching for vulnerabilities in these cells that could allow them to be targeted and killed by immunotherapies, which have so far proven ineffective.


The funding for the groundbreaking project comes from the first joint IASLC–LCRF Team Science Research Grant on the Next Step in the Cure of Oncogene-Driven Lung Cancers. Barbie’s team includes Dana-Farber’s Elliott Brea, MD, PhD; Pasi Jänne, MD, PhD; Eric Smith, MD, PhD; and researchers from two other institutions. Jänne is director of the Belfer Center for Applied Cancer Science and of the Chen-Huang Center for EGFR Mutant Lung Cancers, and the David M. Livingston, MD, Chair at Dana-Farber; Smith is director of translational research for Immune Effector Cell Therapies.

Barbie’s team has discovered certain enzymes that regulate the way DTP cells interact with the body’s immune system and interferons—proteins that play a critical role in helping the immune system combat disease.
“By inhibiting these enzymes, we will test whether this could unleash the immune response against these residual cells, thus eradicating tumors and increasing cure rates,” said Barbie. “It’s a true honor that the LCRF and IASLC have recognized the promise of our research done in collaboration with investigators here and in Japan.”

The LCRF notes that while lung cancer is responsible for more deaths worldwide than any other form of cancer, there have been many advances in the molecular profiling of tumors and FDA approval for new therapies targeting oncogenes—the mutated genes that give rise to cancer. But resistance usually develops, and the disease progresses.

“Being able to stop resistance before it begins would be a lifesaver.”

Antoinette Wozniak, MD, Lung Cancer Research Foundation


“Our goal with this grant is to investigate strategies that will lead to a cure for oncogene-driven lung cancer,” said Antoinette Wozniak, MD, chief scientific officer for LCRF. “Being able to stop resistance before it begins would be a lifesaver. We are confident that this team can move the science forward and potentially change the treatment paradigm for patients.”

title: Reaching across the globe to advance prostate cancer research
body:
Summer 2025
By Elyse Pleickhardt

“A cancer diagnosis takes its toll,” Ross Mayer said, recalling his own battle with an aggressive form of prostate cancer. “Everyone needs a little hope when facing it.”

Mayer found more than hope at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. His oncologist, Mary-Ellen Taplin, MD, treated him with lifesaving surgery, radiation, and hormone therapy. Today Mayer is cancer-free—and offering hope to others with his generous gifts to Dana-Farber.

Through annual gifts and a bequest, Mayer has made a significant gift commitment, establishing The Ross Mayer Endowed Fellowship in Prostate Cancer and the accompanying Mayer Fellow Advancement Fund.

The first ever Ross Mayer research fellow is a natural fit. Aya Abdelnaser, MB, BCh, began her medical schooling in her home country of Egypt, where she focused on prostate cancer. The Mayer Fellow Advancement Fund helped Abdelnaser get funding many young scientists find difficult to secure. Now, Abdelnaser is researching how to identify and treat different types of prostate cancer at Dana-Farber alongside Taplin, Mayer’s trusted partner and chair of Dana-Farber’s Executive Committee for Clinical Research.

At their first meeting, Mayer was overjoyed to hear about Abdelnaser’s enthusiasm for the research, her education, and her family. He was pleased to know her husband and child joined her in Boston as she passionately pursues her research.
Mayer and Abdelnaser recognize that they come from very different places and cultures, yet they have a common goal: finding better treatment options for such a vicious disease together. Social and cultural differences disappear in the name of a cure.

“We need to look for new ways to battle cancer. Research provides patients with more avenues to get better.”

Ross Mayer


“We need to look for new ways to battle cancer,” Mayer said, “to buy time for patients with new technology so they can fight until the next treatment is available. Research provides patients with more avenues to get better.”

A longtime supporter of Dana-Farber, Mayer has also established the Ross Mayer Fund to advance Taplin’s innovative research. He named the Ross Mayer Laboratory Services Bay in the Yawkey Center for Cancer Care, the Ross Mayer Nourishment area in Foxborough, the Roberta Arkin Ring of Hope in the Foxborough Ripple Effect display, Genes in honor of Clair Beard and Dana-Farber oncologists, and has pledged to name Dr. Taplin’s office. Mayer is also a member of the Dana-Farber Society.

Mayer’s newest gifts establishing The Ross Mayer Endowed Fellowship in Prostate Cancer and the Mayer Fellow Advancement Fund further demonstrate his relentless passion for cutting-edge research and lifesaving prostate cancer care.

title: Bekensteins endow investigatorship in honor of Meredith and Billy Starr
body:
Summer 2025
By Mike Quinn
Photography by Pan-Mass Challenge

Josh Bekenstein and his wife, Anita, know that Dana-Farber’s people are its driving force—from trailblazing faculty who transform cancer medicine, to committed supporters who equip these brilliant innovators to do their best work.

Grounded in this core belief, the Bekensteins recently made a generous gift to the Institute to establish the Meredith and Billy Starr Investigatorship. Their gift honors Billy Starr, founder and chairman of the Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), and his wife, Meredith Beaton Starr, PMC director of stewardship. Cigall Kadoch, PhD, a world-renowned biochemist and expert in the understanding of gene regulation, was selected as the inaugural incumbent of the Starr Investigatorship.

For the Starrs, the new investigatorship provides meaningful tribute to their decades-long efforts to bring cures closer by the mile through the PMC—the beloved Massachusetts-based bike-athon and Dana-Farber’s largest single contributor. The PMC raises 66% of the Jimmy Fund’s annual revenue and has raised more than $1 billion for Dana-Farber since 1980. “It’s an immense honor to have an investigatorship named in recognition of my life’s ambition to help one day eradicate cancer,” said Billy. “Meredith and I look forward to witnessing the impact Dr. Kadoch will undoubtedly make on the future of innovation and progress in cancer research and treatment.”

In a challenging funding climate, endowed roles like the Starr Investigatorship are essential for bolstering brilliant research at the Institute and supporting visionary scientists like Kadoch at a crucial point in their careers. Internationally recognized for her work, Kadoch is improving understanding of the biological drivers of disease progression and translating these insights into novel therapeutics. Her laboratory studies large molecular “machines” in the nuclei of our cells that govern DNA architecture and are mutated in over 20% of all cancers. Kadoch’s work has paved the way for first-in-class therapeutic agents applicable to a wide range of adult and pediatric cancers, which are in early stage clinical development. With the resources from the Starr Investigatorship, Kadoch will build on these efforts and pursue even greater advances.

“It is a privilege for Anita and me to celebrate Billy and Meredith Starr, and to support Cigall as she unlocks the next wave of breakthroughs in cancer science and care.”

Josh Bekenstein


Josh Bekenstein, a 33-year PMC rider, member of its board of directors, and chairman of Dana-Farber’s Board of Trustees, underscored the importance of the Starrs’ philanthropic leadership and Kadoch’s pioneering work. “Billy and Meredith have had an amazing career leading the PMC and have done so much for Dana-Farber,” Bekenstein said. “It is a privilege for Anita and me to celebrate them and support Cigall as she unlocks the next wave of breakthroughs in cancer science and care.”

title: Edward P. Evans Foundation takes aim at blood disorders
body:
Summer 2025
By Kathleen Clute
Photography by Sam Ogden

The Edward P. Evans Foundation has awarded $1.65 million in grants to three Dana-Farber researchers studying a group of conditions caused by malfunctioning bone marrow.

Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a group of rare blood disorders in which the bone marrow does not make enough healthy blood cells. Symptoms of MDS can vary but often include fatigue, shortness of breath, easy bruising or bleeding, and increased susceptibility to infections. About 30% of patients with MDS will develop acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

“Finding better treatments for MDS means investing in promising, innovative, and high-impact research,” said Timothy Graubert, MD, president of the Edward P. Evans Foundation. “I have every confidence that the work of these talented Dana-Farber investigators will help us make enormous strides toward a cure.”

“I have every confidence that their work will help us make enormous strides toward a cure.”

Timothy Graubert, MD, Edward P. Evans Foundation


The foundation awarded Lachelle Weeks, MD, PhD, a 2024 Discovery Research Grant for her investigations into clonal hematopoiesis (CH), a precursor of blood cancers such as MDS. Because the chemotherapy and radiation prescribed for various cancers can damage healthy blood and bone marrow cells, some patients develop therapy-related MDS that makes it difficult to safely continue treating the primary cancer. MDS can also arise in cancer survivors as an often fatal side effect of their treatment.


Weeks and her team are studying how CH causes significantly low blood cell counts during treatment with the goal of developing a tool that could identify individuals at high risk for therapy-related MDS and enable future clinical trials.
Nicole Prutsch, PhD, and Michelle Robinette, MD, PhD, received 2024 Evans MDS Young Investigator Awards. Prutsch studies TET2 mutant CH, where TET2 mutant stem cells and inflammatory macrophages increase the risk of MDS and atherosclerosis. Prutsch aims to uncover the key molecular mechanisms that drive this process and identify strategies to reduce inflammation and disease progression.

Robinette’s work focuses on the link between MDS and systemic and inflammatory autoimmune diseases (SIAD). Researchers have long known that people with MDS tend to have more SIAD than the general populace, and that some mutated blood cells can use inflammation signals to grow.

Robinette is studying somatic mutations in the gene UBA1, which lead to severe SIAD as well as MDS, to learn how they cause inflammation in many different organs. She is also researching whether patients with MDS have other mutations that can be linked to SIAD.
The Edward P. Evans Foundation has funded more than $14 million in Dana-Farber research focused on MDS and AML since 2013 and established the Edward P. Evans Center for Myelodysplastic Syndromes at Dana-Farber.

title: Tricking the immune system to defeat cancer
body:
Summer 2025
By Kathleen Clute
Photography by Bryce Vickmark

The New York Stem Cell Foundation (NYSCF) awarded a five-year, $1.5 million grant to Dana-Farber’s Judith Agudo, PhD, for her work to make cancerous tumors more susceptible to immunotherapies and to protect transplanted organs from attack by the immune system.

Agudo received a NYSCF-Robertson Stem Cell Investigator Award, which supports promising early career scientists whose cutting-edge research holds the potential to accelerate treatments and cures. She is a principal investigator in the Department of Cancer Immunology and Virology.

Agudo is using her NYSCF Robertson Award for a project aimed at uncovering the mechanisms that regulate the sensitivity of distinct cells to be recognized, attacked, and killed by the immune system.

“The immune system is a major roadblock in all stem-cell-based therapies for autoimmune disease, as well as for transplantation,” said Agudo. “Identifying strategies to provide transplanted organs with the property of invisibility to the immune system is a critical unmet need in regenerative medicine.”

Deploying technology she developed to study T-cell interactions with other cells, Agudo wants to learn how some healthy cells that are naturally resistant to attack by the immune system can achieve this striking ability. This could lead to the discovery of genes or pathways that can be harnessed safely and effectively to protect transplanted tissues from rejection or to render cancerous cells more vulnerable to immunotherapy.

“My project also has implications for any regenerative approach for autoimmune diseases, such as type 1 diabetes,” said Agudo. “In diseases like this, restored cells inevitably succumb to immune attack unless the immune system is strongly suppressed. But that approach puts patients at high risk for infection and cancer.”

The NYSCF combines the depth of a highly focused disease research institute with the breadth of a wide-ranging philanthropic organization. It has invested more than $450 million in stem cell science since its founding in 2005.

“The NYSCF-Robertson Awards give researchers the flexibility to pursue their boldest ideas while connecting top minds with one another to push the entire field forward,” said Jennifer Raab, the foundation’s president and CEO. “Dr. Agudo’s pioneering work holds great promise for patients with cancer and autoimmune diseases.”

title: Carney family remains steadfast in support of breast cancer research
photo_credit: Photography by Sam Ogden, Jessamyn Martin
body:
Summer 2025
By Robbie Merritt
Photography by Sam Ogden, Jessamyn Martin

With a recent $1 million gift, the Carney Family Charitable Foundation, led by Trustees Patrick and Lillian Carney, has expanded a legacy of support for breast cancer immuno-oncology research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute that spans over 20 years.

This is the latest in a series of gifts dating back to 2004, when the Carney Family first established a partnership with Eric P. Winer, MD, then-chief of the Division of Women’s Cancers, following the loss of beloved family member Virginia Czerny to metastatic breast cancer. In 2016, they established the Carney Family Charitable Foundation Fund for Breast Cancer Immuno-Oncology, helping launch the immuno-oncology program in breast cancer at Dana-Farber. And in 2020, the foundation made gifts to support breast cancer research and Dana-Farber’s Emergency Response Fund, which addressed the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Institute.
Lillian Carney, president of the Carney Family Charitable Foundation, said, “It is with sincere gratitude that the Carney Family Charitable Foundation supports Dana-Farber’s cancer research, and we are proud of the tremendous impact this work has had advancing immune-oncology.”

“We are proud of the tremendous impact this work has had advancing immuno-oncology.”

Lillian Carney, Carney Family Charitable Foundation


The newest gift will continue to bolster breast cancer research at Dana- Farber by supporting the work of Sara Tolaney, MD, MPH, the current chief of the Division of Breast Oncology in the Susan F. Smith Center for Women’s Cancers. Her work focuses on the use of CDK4/6 inhibitors and antibody drug conjugates, the advancement of clinical trials in immunotherapy, and the development of less toxic treatments and therapies for patients with low-risk HER2-positive breast cancer.


“This gift has been transformative,” Tolaney said. “It has allowed us to set up a liquid biopsy program where we can study blood samples and identify patients who may show early signs of breast cancer recurrence. We’re also planning clinical trials to see if novel therapies can be administered to individuals with detectable circulating tumor DNA, with the goal of clearing it and preventing recurrence.”

title: Dakolias gift establishes innovative collaboration in oncology nursing education
body:
Summer 2025
By Caitlin Henault
Photography by Sam Ogden

Nurses are integral to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s ability to provide unmatched cancer care and conduct world-leading research. Through nursing residency and fellowship programs, Dana-Farber trains talented, innovative, and compassionate nurses to join the field of oncology as clinical practitioners, researchers, and nurse-scientists. However, since the COVID-19 pandemic, the United States faces a worsening nursing shortage that could lead to a crisis for medical centers in the coming years, with one million nurses projected to retire by 2030. Also concerning is an insufficient pipeline of qualified nurses to take their place—especially those specifically trained in oncology.

During the pandemic, Dean and Monique Dakolias were incredibly inspired by the dedication of caregivers. As vice-chair of Columbia University’s Board of Trustees, Dean also observed the widespread stress and burnout affecting nurses at the university’s hospital. Recognizing the crucial role health care institutions have in serving the greater good, Dean and Monique set out to strategically leverage their resources to help address the emerging care gap.

Following an introduction to Dana-Farber through longtime friend and colleague Jonathan Lavine, an Institute Trustee, Dean and Monique recognized the growing demand for nurses trained in oncology. With a generous gift of $1 million, they established the Dakolias Family and Lavine Family Fund for Career Development in Nursing to support educational nursing initiatives in collaboration with Northeastern University. This current-use fund, designed to maximize impact and accelerate results, will establish a scholarship program for staff at Dana-Farber who are pursuing degrees in nursing, provide employment opportunities for students in Northeastern’s cooperative education program, and support the development of a dedicated oncology nursing curriculum.

“This gift from the Dakolias family empowers Dana-Farber and Northeastern University to improve access to careers in oncology nursing and build a more diverse workforce through education, employment, and mentorship opportunities,” said Anne Gross, PhD, RN, NEA-BC, FAAN, senior vice president of patient care services, chief nursing officer, and the Ning Zhao Chair of Nursing at Dana-Farber. “These programs will ensure our team of dedicated nurses can continue to deliver exceptional care for years to come.”

While the Dakolias family did not have a personal connection to Dana-Farber, they encourage others to recognize the importance of dedicating resources to health care and educational institutions.

“Institutions that educate and train the next generation of medical professionals are critical to the health and well-being of people across the United States and the globe,” said Dean. “To ensure they thrive, we need to focus our energy and resources on finding innovative ways to support them—especially by facilitating powerful collaborations like this one between Dana-Farber and Northeastern.”

title: Rare eye cancer is focus of new fellowship
body:
Summer 2025
By Kathleen Clute

Every year, about 3,000 Americans are diagnosed with ocular melanoma, a rare cancer that develops in the cells that produce pigment in the eye and is the most common form of eye cancer in adults, according to the American Cancer Society. The disease metastasizes in nearly half of all patients, and accounts for 5% of all melanomas. There is no cure.

Jonathan and Shelley Isaacson have made a $1 million gift to establish Dana-Farber’s first fellowship dedicated to the study of the disease, The Isaacson Family Fellowship in Ocular Melanoma.

The Isaacsons’ motivation was personal—their adult son had been diagnosed and treated for ocular melanoma as a teenager. “When somebody has cancer, the whole family goes through it together,” said Jonathan, chairman and CEO of the Gem Group, Inc., in Lawrence, Mass. “After that experience, we felt the need to get involved and do something. Our research showed that there isn’t a lot of funding for rare cancers, so this seemed like an opportunity.”
Rizwan Haq, MD, PhD, will appoint and mentor the Isaacson Family Fellow to investigate the genetic mutations that drive the disease and identify therapies to target those mutations. Haq is the director of Dana-Farber’s Ocular Melanoma Center.

For the past several years, Jonathan and Shelley have supported the work of Megha Shettigar, PhD, a research fellow in Haq’s lab who is using a revolutionary gene-editing technology known as CRISPR Cas9 to find therapeutic targets for treating melanoma.
Jonathan said he was inspired by his visits to the lab, where he observed “smart, dedicated people working really hard every day to find a solution. It has been very gratifying to support this, and to create an opportunity for a researcher to develop their skill set and become interested in this particular problem.”

“It’s an incredible experience, seeing smart, optimistic people working really hard every day to solve a problem.”

Jonathan Isaacson


The Isaacsons have endowed their family fellowship in perpetuity to ensure that there will always be funding for a fellow to focus on ocular melanoma.

Haq said that the Isaacsons’ support will generate new knowledge, develop the next generation of ocular melanoma experts, and enable important progress. “We need to better understand why melanoma spreads and why treatments don’t always work,” he said. “And to find new treatments when our existing strategies aren’t effective. The Isaacson fellows will help us do that.”

By Kayla McMahon

The Palm Beach community once again demonstrated remarkable generosity by raising over $1.31 million to support Dana-Farber Cancer Institute through their Palm Beach Annual appeal. Funds from the appeal provide essential unrestricted support, enabling Dana-Farber to drive early stage research, develop new treatments, and address the physical, emotional, and spiritual needs of patients.

Dana, whose partnership with Sidney Farber, MD, laid the groundwork for the world-class Institute that Dana-Farber is today. For more than three decades, Palm Beach supporters have helped Dana-Farber make significant strides toward a future free of the burden of cancer, ensuring the best possible outcomes for patients everywhere. Their dedication and generosity are invaluable to Dana-Farber’s ongoing success and innovation.
